# Betting, gaming, lotteries and digital wallets
Status: SEED

## Use when
Sports betting, casinos, fantasy games, lotteries, in-game currency, top-up marketplaces, crypto wallets and exchanges, prepaid card apps.

## Tests (own accounts, minimum stakes)
- Stake and payout: stake negative, zero or fractional; odds from the client; payout computed from client-sent odds; settlement of a bet twice; cash-out value from the client; bet accepted after the event started; bet on a closed market.
- Bonuses: sign-up and deposit bonuses claimed multiple times (email variants, device, payment method); wagering requirements evaluated in the client; withdrawal of bonus balance before requirements.
- Wallet: deposit confirmation trusted from the browser; withdrawal to another user's account; withdrawal limits per user not per method; parallel withdrawals (`race`); balance going negative; refunds of lost bets.
- KYC and responsible gambling: self-exclusion and limits that can be changed without cooling off; underage checks bypassed by skipping steps (`fintech/kyc-onboarding-and-account-opening.md`).
- Randomness and fairness: outcomes seeded from time or client; results predictable from earlier values (`server-side/insecure-randomness-and-secrets-generation.md`); client-side random numbers submitted as results.
- Games and items: item duplication through race, trade or gift windows; selling the same item twice; negative prices; server accepts score or progress from the client.
- Exchanges and crypto: order price and quantity from the client, fee tiers, rounding in quote and base currencies, deposit address reuse, withdrawal address whitelist changes without a delay, internal transfer between users (IDOR), API keys with trade and withdraw permissions mis-scoped.
- Affiliate and promo codes: self-referral, cashback loops (see `logic/promotions-referrals-and-loyalty-abuse.md`).

## Safety
Use minimum stakes. Never move funds that are not yours. Where actions are irreversible (withdrawal), stop at the request that proves the missing check.

# Business logic vulnerabilities (drill patterns)
Status: SEED (original notes from general technique, modelled on the public Web Security Academy topic list; not copied from it)

## Use when
Any flow with rules: shopping, transfers, invites, approvals, pricing.

## Signals
- Client-side validation only; numbers you control; sequence assumptions; roles inferred from the UI.

## Verify safely (bounty-safe: smallest proof, no data dumping, no damage)
Run each drill against the app's own rules; each needs a control showing the rule normally holds.

## Variants to try
- Excessive trust in client-side controls; failing to handle unconventional input (negative, huge, zero, fractional, unicode); inconsistent security controls across features; flawed assumptions about user behaviour; domain-specific flaws (discounts, gift cards); encryption oracles; email parser discrepancies.

## Lab drills (practice pattern: do these on the Academy or a local vulnerable app, never a live target)
- High-level logic flaw; low-level flaw with integer limits; inconsistent handling of exceptional input; weak isolation on dual-use endpoint; password reset broken logic; 2FA broken logic; insufficient workflow validation; authentication bypass through flawed state machine; infinite money logic flaw; encryption oracle; email address parser discrepancy.

## Triage notes
See logic/*.md for the DISTILLED notes; this file is the drill list.

## Lab catalogue
12 Academy labs for this topic with levels, entry points and payload starting points: `training/academy/business-logic-vulnerabilities.md`

files.trigger: Several findings verified: build chains before reporting
files.text:
# Chaining verified findings
Status: SEED

Do this once two or more findings are verified. A chain is worth reporting when the combined impact is clearly higher than the parts, and every link is proven with evidence you already hold.

Common links:
- Info leak (credentials, tokens, ids) then authentication or authorization bypass: debug dump of admin password then admin function. Leaked reset PIN then account takeover then money movement.
- Forgeable token then BFLA: weak JWT secret then forged admin claim then admin routes.
- Mass assignment then logic: client-set balance or role then transfer, loan or approval flows.
- BOLA read then BOLA write: reading another user's id or account number then using it as the target of a transfer, card operation or reset.
- Injection then auth bypass then data access.
- SSRF then metadata or internal admin routes. Stored XSS then admin session action.
- Race then limit bypass: parallel funding or redemption after a read that shows the limit.

How to write a chain: title, the ordered list of finding ids, one paragraph of narrative, the resulting impact in business terms, and which link is the weakest (so the reader knows what to fix first). Use the engine `chain` action; it refuses ids that are not accepted findings.

Do not invent steps you have not proven. A chain that needs an unverified step is a hypothesis: put it in the ledger.

# Cross-industry business logic casebook

Status: SEED
Invariant: the server decides price, identity, order of steps, limits and ownership. Anything the client supplies for these is a suggestion.

## Use when
Any app with money, stock, bookings, points, workflow approval, tenants, or time limits. Pick the section that matches the product, then run the cross-cutting tests at the end. Use your own accounts, small amounts, and test sandboxes.

## Banking and financial services
- Price or tier swapped in the request, or a success token from a cheap purchase reused for an expensive one.
- Amounts with more decimals than allowed; rounding that gains a fraction.
- Cancel a transfer midway: money back in full, or stuck pending?
- Same source and destination account; transfers to self.
- Overdraft by concurrent withdrawals (race on balance).
- Scheduled payment set to a past date; recurring payment with an end date in the past.
- New beneficiary plus large transfer in one session with no cooling-off.
- Exchange rate locked at initiation, or changeable by delaying submission.
- Daily limit enforced per transaction instead of per day (split into many small ones).
- Account freeze bypass through an older session token or a linked account.
- Back-button resubmission of a payment confirmation.
- Step-up authentication for large transfers skipped by calling the confirm endpoint directly.
- Statements before account opening, or another account's statements through `account_id`.

## Payment and checkout
- Discount kept after the cart changes; a 100 percent code applied then removed before payment.
- Negative donation or tip lowering the total.
- Gateway redirect fields (amount, currency) tampered; payment callback replayed or forged.
- Plan id changed from monthly to annual at the monthly price.
- Business discount code used from a consumer account.
- Test card numbers accepted in production.
- Refund greater than the original payment; refund after refund.
- Expired session still completing a payment with stale authorization.

## E-commerce and retail
- Out-of-stock item added by calling the cart API directly.
- Pre-order or ship-date parameters changing commitments.
- Flash-sale price honored after the sale ends (cached price in the request).
- Free sample claimed repeatedly across accounts; `user+1@` aliases for first-order discounts.
- Shared cart or wishlist link exposing billing details or allowing edits.
- Marketplace: buyer address altered between checkout and seller.
- Digital downloads reused after expiry or over the allowed count.
- Add-on fees (gift wrap) removed from the request while the service is still delivered.
- Reviews for products never bought; order tracking page leaking address and phone from an order number.

## Multi-tenant and SaaS
- Tenant id or org id changed to read, edit or delete another tenant's objects.
- Admin of one tenant reaching another tenant's admin screens.
- Removed members keeping access through tokens, sessions or old share links.
- Co-owner demotion that raises the actor's own privileges.
- Paid features reachable on a free plan by calling the API directly; suspended workspaces still working with old keys.
- Imports (CSV) that link records across tenants; invites sent in parallel to exceed seat limits.
- Public keys in the front end used for write operations meant for private keys.

## Healthcare
- Patient id changed to read another patient's records, prescriptions, lab results or exports.
- Booking an already reserved slot; late-cancel fees avoided; mandatory consent skipped.
- Patient editing clinical notes or medication history through a writable field.
- Provider reading records of patients not assigned to them.
- Lab results visible before the clinician releases them.

## HR, payroll and operations
- Employee changing their own salary, grade or bank details without the approval step.
- Approving your own leave, expense or purchase order by setting the approver id.
- Overlapping or negative leave days; duplicate receipts in several claims.
- Payroll run triggered outside the schedule; backdated commission recalculation.
- Terminated users keeping tokens or SSO sessions; managers reading salaries outside their line.
- Onboarding steps (background check) skipped by opening the next stage.

## Gaming, gambling and rewards
- Premium currency credit changed in the success response.
- Locked achievements granted by calling the award endpoint; impossible scores accepted.
- Loot or reward grants replayed; results decided on the client.
- Bonus rounds regranted after disconnect; daily rewards claimed again by changing the device clock or timezone.
- Referral bonus kept after the referred account is deleted.
- Bets cancelled after the outcome is known; tournament entry fee reused.

## Logistics and delivery
- Address changed after dispatch; two drivers accepting one job at once.
- Negative inventory; labels printed for another seller's order.
- Delivered status reset to earlier statuses; proof of delivery sent before arrival.
- Second refund on a return already refunded; picks marked for items not on the list.
- Payout inflated by claiming a different zone.

## Travel, booking and ticketing
- Seat holds extended forever; hold expiry racing payment.
- Non-refundable ticket refunded with a hidden `refund_type` field.
- Loyalty points kept after cancelling the trip.
- Eligibility discounts (child, senior, military) not checked; group fare kept after reducing passengers.
- Upgrade price set to zero; double booking of the same room by concurrent requests.
- Queue tokens shared to skip the line; free-cancellation window measured from the wrong timestamp.

## Social and content platforms
- `verified` or `is_verified` accepted from a normal profile update.
- Private posts readable through the direct API; blocked users still seeing content.
- Follower or engagement inflation by follow and unfollow loops.
- Paywalled content readable by its creator's free account or by direct URL.
- Report-spam to take down a competitor; freed usernames reused for impersonation.
- Deleted content re-shared from a cached id; tips reversible after payout.

## Crypto and digital wallets
- Address validated against the wrong network; transfers replayed.
- Staking rewards for partial periods; simultaneous buy and sell wash trades.
- Referral commission surviving withdrawal and refund.
- Slippage tolerance set absurdly high without a warning.
- Withdrawal OTP reused across several withdrawals; whitelist bypass with a flag in the request.

## Time and process
- Login timing differences between valid and invalid users.
- Price frozen in a held request and released after the market moves.
- Holds, OTP windows and sessions: exact expiry plus a short grace; is it strict?
- Used reset links still working after repeated requests.
- Endpoints that trigger background jobs (reports, invoices, exports) flooded in parallel.
- Quotes (insurance, loan) accepted after they expire.

## Abuse defences
- Anomalous bursts that never trigger a lock or alert; lockout applied per device but not per account (or the reverse).
- Geographic or IP restrictions that headers can fake.
- Flagged accounts still receiving full service.
- UI-only restrictions (disabled buttons, hidden fields) that the API does not enforce.
- Content and API rate limits that are absent, or per-endpoint but not per-account.

## Cross-cutting tests
1. Repeat the request with a changed id, price, role, status, count, or date.
2. Replay the same request later, in parallel, and out of order.
3. Skip a step by calling the final endpoint first.
4. Compare the same action across roles, plans and tenants.
5. Check the notification and audit trail: did the system record what happened?

# E-commerce and marketplace logic
Status: SEED

## Use when
Online shops, marketplaces, ticketing, food delivery, classifieds, flash sales, digital goods, subscription boxes.

## Tests
- Cart and price: price, discount, shipping, tax and currency from the client; quantity negative, zero, fractional, huge; changing cart contents after the coupon or after the payment redirect; same item at two prices (variant ids).
- Checkout state: skip steps (address, shipping, payment) by calling the final step; two carts and one payment; paying for cart A and confirming cart B (`payments/payment-gateway-testing.md`).
- Inventory and holds: reservation without payment locking stock (denial of inventory), release rules, flash sale limits per user bypassed by multiple accounts, parallel purchase of the last unit (`logic/inventory-and-allocation-abuse.md`).
- Orders: IDOR on order, invoice, address, tracking; edit shipping address after dispatch; cancel after delivery; return and refund abuse; reselling vouchers.
- Marketplace roles: buyer versus seller versus admin; a seller editing another seller's listing, price or payout account; changing payout details without step-up; seller refunds to own accounts; fake reviews and rating manipulation (rate limits, one per purchase).
- Seller payout and commission: commission rate from the client, negative commission, payout before dispute window, payout currency change.
- Reviews and messaging: stored XSS, HTML injection, links to phishing in buyer-seller chat, buyer contact data exposure.
- Digital goods: download links shareable and unexpiring, license keys enumerable, gift cards and codes (`logic/promotions-referrals-and-loyalty-abuse.md`).
- Search and scraping: price scraping, unreleased products visible by id, draft listings.
- Third-party integrations: shipping and tax APIs trusted blindly, webhooks from payment and logistics (`api/webhooks-and-callbacks.md`).
- Guest checkout: order lookup by order number and email only (enumeration), account takeover by pre-registration with the guest email.

## Report
Order or cart ids, amounts before and after, the endpoint that trusted the client.

files.trigger: Schools, hospitals, government and registries
files.text:
# Education, health and government portals
Status: SEED

## Use when
School and university systems (student records, results, fees), hospitals and clinics, insurance and NHIS-style portals, civil registries, tax and customs, licences, e-government services, NGOs and donor platforms. These hold large amounts of personal data, and they are often built quickly by small vendors.

## Tests
- Record access by predictable id: student number, patient number, national or voter id, application reference. Unauthenticated or low-privilege access to thousands of records is the common critical finding (`api/enumeration-oracles-and-data-scraping.md`, `authz/idor-bola.md`).
- Roles: student, parent, teacher, admin, clerk, doctor, nurse, pharmacist. Parent seeing other children, teacher editing grades or fees for other classes, clerk exporting everything (`authz/privilege-escalation.md`).
- Write endpoints without authentication: update teacher or student details, change grades, mark fees paid, update prescriptions, issue certificates, approve applications.
- Payments: fee payment pages that trust a success return, receipts for unpaid fees, waivers and scholarships set by the client (`payments/payment-gateway-testing.md`).
- Documents: certificates, transcripts, ID scans, medical files by predictable URL or storage listing; forged certificate generation with QR codes that validate nothing.
- Uploads: results spreadsheets, CSV import with formula injection, document uploads with weak validation (`web/file-parsers-and-document-processing.md`).
- Sensitive data in responses: national id, phone, diagnoses, grades, home address; API responses returning whole objects.
- Admin and tooling: exposed runbooks and deployment documents, database credentials in docs and repos, BaaS and CMS libraries with PII or backups (`server-side/baas-and-cms-exposure.md`, `cloud/ci-cd-and-supply-chain.md`).
- GraphQL and APIs: unauthenticated reads and mutations (`advanced/graphql-attacks.md`).
- Legal framing: personal data of minors and health data carry heavy obligations under data protection law (Ghana Data Protection Act 2012 and similar). Name the law and the class of data in the report; rate by population size and sensitivity.

## Safety
Prove with two or three consented or own records and the total count from API metadata. Do not download real personal records.

# HR, payroll, insurance, logistics and procurement logic
Status: SEED

## Use when
Payroll and HR systems, expense tools, insurance quote and claims portals, pension and benefits, freight and warehouse systems, procurement and invoicing.

## Tests
- Payroll and expenses: changing bank details of an employee (self or other) without step-up; approving own expense or timesheet; approver chain skipped; amounts and currencies from the client; duplicate claims; payslip IDOR; export of all salaries by a low role.
- Insurance: quote parameters from the client (age, vehicle value, risk class) changing the premium after calculation; policy purchase without payment confirmation; claim on a cancelled or not-yet-active policy; claim amount above the limit; document upload IDOR; beneficiary change without verification.
- Pensions and benefits: balance and contribution editing, withdrawal requests for others, eligibility computed in the client.
- Logistics: tracking number enumeration revealing addresses and phone numbers; status updates by anyone with the tracking id; label and manifest forgery; delivery confirmation codes with short length and no lockout; changing the consignee after dispatch.
- Procurement and invoicing: vendor bank-detail change without call-back verification (business email compromise assistance in-app), invoice approval by the submitter, purchase orders above limit through splitting, duplicate vendor creation.
- Reports and exports: whole-company exports through a parameter, scheduled reports sent to external emails, shared links without expiry.
- Integrations: ERP and accounting connectors with stored credentials, webhooks that change status.

## Report
The business consequence first: unauthorized payment, wrong payout, forged claim. Then the exact request pair.

files.title: Invariant thinking: how to find logic flaws on purpose
files.trigger: How to find logic flaws on purpose (invariants, state machine, seams)
files.text:
# Invariant thinking: how to find logic flaws on purpose
Status: DISTILLED (method; the same one the engine is built around)

## Use when
You are facing a feature with money, state or permissions and no scanner will find the bug. This is the method I would follow as an auditor.

## 1. Write the invariants (the rules that must always be true)
Examples: "a user sees only their own accounts", "the sum of debits equals the sum of credits", "a paid order cannot be paid again", "a code is used once", "only an approver can approve and not their own request", "the price comes from the server", "a closed account cannot transact", "limits apply per user across all channels". Write 10 to 20 per feature from documentation, the UI, and common sense. Each invariant is one test.

## 2. Draw the state machine
List states (draft, pending, approved, paid, refunded, closed) and transitions with who may trigger them. Then test every illegal transition: skip, repeat, reverse, run from another role, run twice at once.

## 3. Find where each rule is enforced
UI only? One endpoint but not its sibling (mobile API, old version, bulk, import, export, GraphQL, websocket)? Only at one step (the final confirm) but not the others? A rule enforced in two places usually differs between them; diff the two.

## 4. Attack the seams
- Between components: the front end and the core, the gateway and the service, two microservices, the app and the payment provider.
- Between time and state: race windows, retries, timeouts, partial failures, delayed callbacks.
- Between identities: user A's object with user B's token, a role change mid-flow, a deleted user's leftover sessions, tenant switches.
- Between formats: JSON versus form, number versus string, array versus scalar, Unicode lookalikes, case, whitespace, rounding.

## 5. Always keep a control
Every test has a control: the same action done legitimately. The difference between the two is the finding. Without the control you cannot show impact.

## 6. Prove at the lowest level that shows the rule broke
Two own accounts, small amounts, before and after states. Stop there.

## 7. Estimate impact in the language of the owner
"A customer can move up to X per day out of another customer's account" beats "IDOR on /transfer". Name data class, money, affected population, preconditions and detection.

## What scanners miss and humans (and models) can catch
Anything that needs knowing what the app is for. This is why the autopilot is paired with a model that reads the app model: the model proposes invariants, the engine enforces evidence, scope and request limits.

files.text:
# Inventory and allocation abuse (denial of inventory)
Status: DISTILLED
Trigger: bookings, reservations, seats, stock holds, quotas, trial slots, anything that becomes unavailable before payment or confirmation.
Source: WSTG 10-Business_Logic 11 (distilled in own words).

## Invariants to test
- A resource should become unavailable only after a commitment (payment, verification), or hold for a bounded time.
- One customer should have a cap on concurrent holds, across all booking paths and reservation states.
- Cancel or expiry must release the resource.

## Tests
1. Map the functions: display, hold, confirm, cancel or release.
2. Start a hold and never finish. From a second session check availability and when it is released.
3. Check whether the per-customer cap applies to every path (web, API, mobile, different states) or only one.
4. Cancel a normal reservation and verify it returns to the pool.
5. Prove impact on a second eligible customer with a very small sample. Use designated test inventory and agree limits with the owner. Extrapolate in the report; do not drain real inventory.

## Evidence
Two sessions, timestamps, availability before and after, release behaviour.

# Plan gating, quotas and limit bypass

Status: DISTILLED (reports H1 3591764, 3102890, 3104355, 3370430, 3369843, 3371448, 3114554)
Invariant: paid features, role choices and quotas are enforced on the server at the moment of use, counting everything that can consume them (pending, in flight, cloned).

## Signals
- Free vs Pro vs Enterprise features, seat or project limits, "upgrade to enable" prompts, workspace visibility, invite roles, agents or models enabled by an admin for a time.

## Tests
1. Replay the request that the UI blocks for your plan; flip the field the UI toggles (role, visibility, plan feature) directly in the API.
2. Toggle and revert: change the setting to a blocked value in the UI, intercept, and send the final state (some flows validate only one transition).
3. Seats and limits: count what the check counts. Invite more users than the limit while invites are pending, then let them all accept (limit checked at invite time, not at accept time).
4. Races on creation limits (folders, projects, orgs): send parallel creates.
5. Cloning and copying: an admin-enabled resource (model, agent, template) copied by a member keeps working after the admin disables the original. Test by changing the id or sid inside the update request.
6. Low roles toggling admin-only workspace features (AI features, visibility) through the settings API.

## Evidence
State read back showing the paid feature, role or count above the plan, plus the control showing the UI refusing it.

## Reporting notes
Programs often rate these low or informative unless money or licensing loss is clear. State the revenue effect (seats not purchased, features not paid for) and the scale when repeated.

## More patterns (batch 04)
- Pending invites not counted toward a seat cap (Dust 3102890); folder cap raced (3104355).
- Paid-only options set by editing the request body: project visibility, read-only role on free plan (Lovable).
- Cap or uniqueness enforced in the UI only: organizations with the same name by race (informative), vote once per user (Urban Dictionary).
- Single-use discount, loyalty claim, reward or coupon reused (Stripe fee discount, Vend loyalty, H1 reward redemption, AWS merch coupon).

files.title: Price, quantity and value tampering
files.trigger: Price, quantity, currency or discount accepted from the client
files.text:
# Price, quantity and value tampering

Status: SEED
Invariant: the server computes price, totals, discounts and credits from its own data, never from client values.

## Signals
- Request carries price, amount, total, quantity, currency, plan_id, wallet_id, discount or fee fields.
- Payment is confirmed by a client redirect or a client-supplied status.
- Cart or order total shown in the UI differs from what the payment step receives.

## Tests
1. Negative and zero quantity or amount; fractions; very large numbers; scientific notation.
2. Change plan, SKU or wallet id to a cheaper or someone else's id while keeping the paid amount.
3. Change currency code or exchange rate fields; pay in a weak currency for a strong one.
4. Edit the amount between checkout and the payment provider callback (in-flight modification).
5. Remove fee, tax or cancellation lines from the request body.
6. Apply a discount or coupon repeatedly, or stack incompatible ones.
7. Pay a small amount, then complete an order or top up a larger value.
8. Replay a successful payment confirmation against a different order.

## Distilled variants (from ingested reports)
- Signed requests are not safe if the signature concatenates fields without delimiters. Test boundary shifting (move characters between a field name and its value) and parameter injection through any user text field that is copied into the signed request (email, name, description). Source: H1 1295844.

- Dynamic pricing manipulation: if prices react to demand or user behavior, start actions that never complete payment (for example open bookings) to push the price, then repeat at scale. Impact framing: revenue loss or uncompetitive prices. Source: YesWeHack top hunter methodology for CWE-840 (web page, own words).

## Evidence
Order or balance read back from the account showing a value that does not match what was paid.

## Seed reports (ranked public index, title only until distilled)
H1 771694 negative quantity price; 364843 negative quantity total; 512968 and 614523 order amount manipulation; 1295844 modify data sent to payment provider; 1408782 wallet top up with arbitrary payment; 511044 and 938021 free membership by plan or wallet id tampering.

## Business logic checklist (PayloadsAllTheThings, WSTG; distilled)
- Reviews: rating outside the scale (0, 6, negative), reviewing without purchase as "verified", many reviews per user (race), reviewing as another user, unprotected CSRF, any extension in review uploads.
- Discount codes: reuse, race a one-time code across two accounts, parameter pollution or mass assignment to stack codes, apply to excluded items by editing the request.
- Fees: negative delivery or service fee, flag or parameter that zeroes shipping.
- Currency: pay in one currency, refund in another, keep the rate difference.
- Premium: hit premium endpoints without plan, buy then cancel or refund and check access remains, flip true/false entitlement flags in responses or local storage, repeat cancellation to get repeated refunds.
- Cart: negative quantity on one item to offset another, quantity above stock, moving or removing items in another user's cart.
- Comments or one-per-user actions: race for several, forge verified-user parameters.
- Rounding: amounts below the minimum precision where the sender is rounded down to zero and the receiver rounded up (money from nothing, looped by script). Source: H1 176461.
- Integrity checks (WSTG): hidden fields, non-editable fields you can still submit, and system components like logs where you can write what you should only read.
- Function use limits (WSTG): list every action meant to happen once or N times, then try back and forth navigation, cart load and unload for extra discounts, and cancel after credit.

## PortSwigger logic flaw themes (distilled)
Client-side control trust (change values after the browser checks); unconventional input (negative, huge, long, wrong type; note limits and truncation: a stored email cut at 255 characters can turn a lookalike domain into a privileged one); flawed assumptions (remove parameters one by one, skip, repeat or reorder steps); domain-specific (reach a state where an adjustment no longer matches its criteria, for example add items to hit a discount then remove them); encryption oracles (user input encrypted and returned, reuse that ciphertext elsewhere).

files.trigger: Promos, referrals, gift cards, loyalty
files.text:
# Promotions, referrals, gift cards and loyalty abuse
Status: SEED

## Use when
Coupons, promo codes, referral bonuses, cashback, loyalty points, gift cards, vouchers, welcome credits, trial periods.

## Tests (own accounts)
- Single-use codes: reuse across accounts, parallel redemption (`race`), redemption on a cancelled order, redemption twice by changing case or adding whitespace (`CODE`, `code `).
- Stacking: multiple codes at once, code plus sale price, code plus points, order edits after the discount is applied.
- Minimum spend and category rules: add items, apply the code, remove items before payment.
- Value: discount percentages above 100, negative values, fixed discounts larger than the total, free orders turned into credits.
- Referral: self-referral with a second email, same device, same payment method; referral count tamper; bonus paid before the referee's qualifying action; referral link parameters trusted from the client.
- Gift cards: code format and entropy (enumeration by guessing against a rate limit), balance check endpoint without limit, transfer of balance between cards in a loop, refunds to gift cards then cash out.
- Loyalty points: earn on refunded orders, earn rate set by the client, redeem more points than owned (race), points transferable then recalled.
- Trial abuse: unlimited trials by re-registering with email variants (`+` aliases, dots).

## Report
Show balances before and after with amounts, and why the rule is meant to prevent it.

files.title: Races and double spend
files.trigger: Balance, credits, coupons, gift cards, payouts, one-time actions
files.text:
# Races and double spend

Status: SEED
Invariant: one-time and balance-limited actions succeed at most once, even under concurrency.

## Signals
- Gift cards, coupons, referral bonuses, credits, withdrawals, payouts, votes, invites, limited stock.
- Check then act pattern with a delay (read balance, then debit).

## Tests
1. Send 10 to 30 identical requests at once (single-packet or parallel threads) for redeem, withdraw, apply coupon.
2. Race two different endpoints that touch the same balance (withdraw plus transfer).
3. Race a state change against its validation (disable 2FA while verifying a code).
4. Re-use a consumed token or code right after use and during the processing window.
5. Use the program's test allowance only; never move real funds beyond it.

## Distilled variants (from ingested reports)
- Gift card or voucher redeem endpoint: a burst of about 30 gated simultaneous requests produced several successes (25 dollar card paid out 7 times). Read the balance after the burst. This is a well known test, so expect duplicates unless the feature is new. Source: H1 759247.

## Evidence
Balance or counter read back showing more than one success, with request timings.

## Seed reports
H1 307239 double payout; 759247 gift card redeemed many times; 1849626 fee discount redeemed repeatedly; 2598548 2FA bypass by race; 381356 client-side race condition.

## Race taxonomy and mechanics (PortSwigger research, YesWeHack guide, WSTG; distilled)
Pick the type first, it decides the request set.
- **Limit overrun**: check-then-update gap. Single-use coupon, gift card, vote, invite, rate limit, withdrawal. Burst the same request.
- **Hidden multi-step sequence**: one request passes through short internal states (user created, then flags set). A second request landing in that window sees the weak state, for example MFA not yet enforced.
- **Multi-endpoint**: two different endpoints touching one object. Classic: change the cart after payment is validated but before the order is confirmed. Warm up connections first so the slower endpoint does not lose the race.
- **Single-endpoint**: same endpoint, different values, colliding in shared storage such as the session. Example: two reset or email-change requests for different accounts at once, so one token ends up bound to the other identity.
- **Partial construction**: hit the object while half built, before a secret field is set. Send empty, null or empty-array values so they match the uninitialised column.
- **Time-sensitive tokens**: tokens derived from a timestamp only. Two requests in the same instant yield identical tokens.
- **Session-based locking**: some frameworks serialise requests per session, hiding the bug. Use a different session per request to bypass the serialisation.

Delivery: HTTP/2 single-packet attack (withhold last frame of each request, release together, 20 to 30 requests) removes jitter. HTTP/1.1 uses last-byte sync. Turbo Intruder (gate plus HTTP/2 engine) or Burp parallel send groups do both. Timing is probabilistic, so repeat.
Confirm: show the constraint was actually exceeded (balance, counter, applied discount), not just duplicate 200s. Fresh account per try to avoid state pollution.
Targets: redeem and apply, checkout, transfers, token and code generation and verification, signup uniqueness, anything that reads a value, checks it, then writes it.
Fix to suggest: atomic transactions or row locks, uniqueness constraints, idempotency keys, no sub-states on sensitive endpoints.
Novelty note: plain coupon bursts are heavily hunted. Multi-endpoint and single-endpoint token races on new features are less likely to be duplicates.


## From real reports
Top-voted disclosed reports for this class: `knowledge-base/training/reports/race.md`; patterns in own words: `training/report-patterns.md` (section race); search all 16,024 in the Library Reports tab.

Status: SEED

## Use when
Ride and delivery apps, courier and freelancer marketplaces, field services, rental and booking platforms.

## Tests
- Trip and order pricing: fare, surge, distance and time computed on the server? Client-submitted coordinates and route used for pricing; cancel and re-request to avoid surge; promo codes on one trip used twice; payment method switched after the ride.

- Wallet and tips: tipping or refunding to yourself, negative tips, wallet top-up through the "unlimited balance" pattern of trusting the payment-return page (`payments/payment-gateway-testing.md`).
- Documents and verification: driver licence and vehicle documents (`authz/file-and-document-access-control.md`), verification status set by the client.
- Privacy: rider phone numbers, home addresses and trip history across accounts; masked numbers that can be unmasked; live-location endpoint without authorization.
- Ratings and disputes: rating tampering, dispute and refund creation for trips you were not on.
- Booking and rental: double booking, price change between quote and confirm, free cancellation window bypass, deposits and holds.
- Ops and admin: dispatcher consoles reachable from the public app host, test accounts in production.

## Proof
Two own accounts (rider and driver), a short test trip with before and after wallet states.

# Rule-based business logic testing
Status: SEED

## Use when
You have no model, or tokens are short, and the system moves money, orders, bookings or points. These rules run on the requests already seen with a signed-in test account.

## What runs
- System type guess from endpoints and field names: banking, payment, shop, wallet, telco, booking, gaming, SaaS, health, HR.
- Values the browser decides: price, total, discount, role, plan sent from the client.
- Transfer to the same account; a past or back-dated schedule (a garbage date must be rejected, a past one accepted); an unknown currency code; completing a payment, order or approval with a reference the server never issued; the same discount code applied twice.
- Number tampering, replay and races through the standard probe matrix, when the profile allows them.

## How to read a result
A rule only reports when the changed request is accepted while a control behaves as expected (a garbage value is rejected, a safe twin refuses). Accepted does not always mean exploitable: confirm the ledger or total really changed.

## What it cannot do
It does not understand your product's own rules (cooling-off periods, tiered limits, approval chains). For each checklist scenario the Checklist view lists the most likely requests so you or a model can test them by hand.

# SaaS and B2B platform logic
Status: SEED

## Use when
Multi-tenant products: CRM, HR, project tools, analytics, e-signature, helpdesk, admin consoles, API platforms, white-label products (see how a Wizer-style or LMS vendor hosts many clients).

## Tests
- Tenant isolation: tenant id in path, header, token, subdomain or body; switch it; list endpoints without tenant filter; search and export crossing tenants; cache keys without tenant (`authz/tenant-isolation.md`).
- Roles and invites: invite as admin when you are member, role field in invite acceptance, invite links not bound to email, expired invites still valid, removed users with live tokens, owner transfer flow.
- Seats, plans, quotas: seat limit enforced only at invite creation; downgrade keeps premium features; trial extension; usage metering edited by the client (`logic/plan-and-limit-bypass.md`).
- API keys and tokens: keys scoped to tenant and role? Key listing shows full values? Rotation invalidates the old one? Keys in URLs and logs.
- Integrations and webhooks: OAuth app grants scopes beyond the user's; marketplace apps with broad permission; webhook secrets readable by low roles (`api/webhooks-and-callbacks.md`).
- White-label and custom domains: domain verification takeover (claim another tenant's custom domain), cookie scope across customer subdomains (`web/cookies-subdomains-and-session-scope.md`), subdomain takeover on customer CNAMEs.
- Import and export: CSV and Excel import with formula or XXE, mass assignment through import (set owner, role, balance), export of other tenants' rows, file storage keys without tenant prefix (`web/file-parsers-and-document-processing.md`).
- Audit logs and admin actions: logs editable by tenant admins, impersonation features without consent logging, support access without time limit.
- Billing: plan change without payment, invoice IDOR, payment method change by non-owner, free tier abuse for compute.
- SSO: tenant-specific IdP configuration injection, domain-based auto-join to the wrong tenant, JIT provisioning with unverified emails (`authn/saml-entra-google-sso.md`).
- Background jobs and webhooks reading data under the wrong tenant context; shared queues, shared caches, shared search indices.

## Report
Two tenants you control, the request crossing the boundary, the data or action reached.

files.text:
# Standards-based and business-rule checks (the "4 boxes instead of 6" family)

Some flaws are not a bug in code. The app works exactly as built, but the rule it enforces is weaker than the accepted standard or weaker than the business needs. A scanner cannot know the rule, so the tester must carry it. Each row: the rule, why it matters, how to check safely, what the tool does about it.

Status: DISTILLED from public standards (sources at the end). Tool support is marked: AUTO (the engine looks by itself), HINT (the engine points, a human confirms), MANUAL.

| # | Rule | Why | Safe check | Tool |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | One-time codes sent by SMS, email or app: at least 6 decimal digits, random, single use, short life (10 minutes at most) | 4 digits is 10,000 guesses. With no lockout that is minutes of work. NIST puts the floor at six digits and ten minutes | Count the input boxes or `maxlength` on the code field. Read the API schema for `minLength`/`maxLength`. Never brute force a real account to prove it | AUTO: flags 4-digit or shorter code fields and boxes; HINT for the rest |
| 2 | Wrong-code attempts are limited (lockout or backoff) and the limit is shared across servers, sessions and IPs | A long code with no limit still falls; a short one falls fast | 5 wrong codes on your own test account, watch for 429, lockout or a growing delay | AUTO (no-throttle burst on the code route) |
| 3 | A code works once and expires | Reuse or a long window gives time to guess and to replay | Use a test code twice; check expiry text and response | MANUAL |
| 4 | Code is random, not a counter, timestamp or a value the API returns | Predictable codes need no guessing | Request two codes on a test account and compare; check that the response does not echo the code | HINT |
| 5 | The same strength applies on every channel (web, mobile API, call-centre, USSD, alternative login) | Attackers use the weakest door | Repeat the check on each channel the bank offers | MANUAL |
| 6 | OAuth: redirect URI compared by exact string match against the registered value | Loose matching leaks codes and tokens to an attacker | Look at the authorize link and the discovery document; only the owner of the client may test variations | AUTO (discovery and link review), MANUAL for variations |
| 7 | OAuth: `state` present and checked; PKCE used for the code flow | No `state` allows login CSRF; no PKCE allows code theft and replay | Read authorize URLs in pages and discovery metadata | AUTO |
| 8 | OAuth: no implicit grant (`response_type=token`), no password grant | Tokens in URLs leak through history and Referer headers; password grant hands the password to the client | Read authorize links and `response_types_supported` / `grant_types_supported` | AUTO |
| 9 | Money and single-use actions are atomic (coupon, refund, transfer, reward) | Parallel requests pass the same check before it is updated | Small parallel burst on a test account only | AUTO (race probe) |
| 10 | Workflow order is enforced on the server (pay before confirm, approve before release) | Calling the last step first skips the checks | Call later steps directly on a test account | HINT |
| 11 | Values that carry money (price, fee, rate, limit, currency) are decided by the server | Client-side values are attacker-controlled | Change them on a test account | AUTO (numbers probe) |
| 12 | Recovery paths are not weaker than login (reset by PIN, security question, call-centre bypass) | Recovery is a second login | Compare the factors needed | MANUAL |
| 13 | Account enumeration is not possible by different messages or timings | Lets attackers pick real targets | Compare responses for known and unknown test users | HINT |
| 14 | Limits on amount, count and frequency exist and are enforced for every channel | Missing limits turn small flaws into large losses | Try a value just over the limit on a test account | HINT |

## Why four digits is a real finding and not a style opinion
- Four digits is 10^4 = 10,000 possibilities, six is 10^6 = 1,000,000: a hundred times more work.
- The standard is explicit about the floor: "at least six decimal digits" for server-generated out-of-band secrets (NIST SP 800-63B).
- Impact depends on the second rule: if wrong attempts are limited, a short code is low severity; if they are not, it is account takeover. Report them together, and say which one you proved.
- Banks add a regulatory angle: weak recovery or step-up is a control failure, not only a bug.

## Reporting guidance
- Say which rule, which standard, what you observed (a screenshot of the four boxes or the `maxlength`), and what you did NOT do (no brute force of real accounts).
- Severity: short code alone, low to medium. Short code plus no lockout on a login or money step, high.
- Many programs treat "weak password policy" or "no rate limit" as out of scope. Check the policy first and report the account-takeover impact, not the policy gap.

## Sources
- NIST SP 800-63B (out-of-band secret length and lifetime): https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators and the summary at https://bird.com/explained/verify/how-long-should-an-otp-be-valid-and-how-many-digits.md
- RFC 9700, OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice (exact redirect URI matching, implicit grant, PKCE): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html
- OWASP Top 10 for Business Logic Abuse (action limit overrun, concurrent workflow order bypass): https://owasp.org/projects/top-10-for-business-logic-abuse
- OWASP business logic vulnerability overview (privilege escalation via workflow gaps, discount abuse, race conditions; CWE-841, CWE-642): https://owasp.org/www-community/vulnerabilities/Business_logic_vulnerability
- OWASP Web Security Testing Guide, Business Logic Testing (weak reset, weaker authentication in alternative channels): https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/v42/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/10-Business_Logic_Testing/

# Telco, airtime, data bundles and subscription logic
Status: SEED

## Use when
Mobile operators (MTN, Vodafone/Telecel, AirtelTigo style), MVNOs, ISPs, VAS and content providers, any product sold as airtime, bundles, minutes, subscriptions or recurring plans. Applies to the operator app, self-care portal, dealer or agent app, USSD menus and partner APIs.

## Asset and flow map
Subscriber (MSISDN, SIM, KYC tier) -> wallet or airtime balance -> products (bundles, voice, data, VAS subscriptions) -> channels (app, USSD, SMS keywords, web, dealer, retailer top-up, partner API) -> billing and rating -> notifications. Bugs live in the gap between channels: each channel re-implements the same rule.

## Tests (own numbers only)
- Channel parity: buy or activate the same product through app, USSD, SMS keyword and web; compare price, eligibility, limits, validity and refunds. The cheapest or least checked channel sets the real policy.
- Price and bundle selection: product id, price, validity and bonus accepted from the client; downgrade or upgrade proration; buy a high-value bundle with a low-value product id; negative quantity; currency or unit confusion (MB versus GB, minutes versus seconds).
- Balance and credit: airtime transfer ("share", "borrow", "me2u") with limits, negative or fractional amounts, parallel transfers (`race`), borrowing then clearing the loan to reset limits, transfer to self through two numbers in a loop.
- Promotions: bonus data or airtime on first top-up, referral and "double data" campaigns: claim twice, claim for numbers you do not own, claim after cancellation (see `logic/promotions-referrals-and-loyalty-abuse.md`).
- Subscriptions: auto-renewal and cancel. Can you cancel another subscriber's service by MSISDN (BOLA)? Does cancel really stop billing? Opt-in without consent (VAS subscription created by a web click or by a GET request from another site: CSRF on subscribe).
- SIM and number lifecycle: SIM registration with someone else's ID number, SIM replacement and swap request flows, number porting requests, recycled numbers inheriting services or balances (`fintech/sim-swap-and-telco-dependency.md`).
- Self-care and dealer portals: lookup of any MSISDN's profile, balance, last transactions, ID number and address (enumeration oracles: `api/enumeration-oracles-and-data-scraping.md`); dealer commission calculation and float top-up logic; agent can see all subscribers.
- Mobile money integration: wallet funding from airtime, airtime purchase from wallet, bill pay; reversal paths; see `payments/mobile-money-and-ussd.md`.
- Short codes and USSD: menu options differ per code; extended codes (`*800*4001#`) reach hidden services; test each with `tools/ussd_test.py` (`payments/ussd-banking-and-gateway-security.md`).
- SMS and OTP APIs: partner SMS APIs that let a customer send messages with arbitrary sender ids (spoofing) or without rate limits; OTP sent to the number given in the request.
- Billing and rating: usage records edited by API; zero-rated URLs or sponsored data that can be abused through proxying; roaming and international rates; post-paid credit limit changes.
- Corporate and bulk portals: bulk top-up files (CSV injection, negative lines), enterprise admin roles, sub-account spending limits.

## Proof
Two own numbers, before and after balances and product lists for each channel, and the price per unit the customer actually paid.

# Verification flaws (OTP, email, phone)

Status: SEED
Invariant: a code proves control of one specific contact for one specific action, is limited in attempts, and never leaks.

## Signals
- SMS or email codes at signup, login, change phone, change email, withdrawal.
- Short numeric codes, no visible lockout, code returned in the response or in logs.

## Tests
1. Brute force feasibility: attempt count, lockout, per-IP vs per-account limits, resets by changing a parameter.
2. Code in the API response, in a header, or in the page source.
3. Blank, null, array or wrong-type code values; code for account A accepted for account B.
4. Change the phone or email in the verification request after the code was issued.
5. Reuse after success; use after expiry; use across flows (login code on password reset).
6. Skip the verification step and call the next endpoint (see workflow-step-skipping).

## Evidence
Verified state for a contact you do not control (use your own second contact), plus the attempt count that worked.

## Seed reports
H1 2588329 phone number takeover via change-number OTP; 3255473 OTP bypass at signup; 743545 recovery code brute force; 700612 and 922418 SMS code brute force; 897385 2FA bypass with blank code; 699082 OTP bypass for settings; 2635315 OTP leaked in API response; 921780 login as other user via otp endpoints.

## More patterns (batch 04)
- Verification parameter omitted entirely completes signup (Tucows hover).
- Email change without verification keeping old sessions (DoD); verified without inbox access (X); invite key shown to the inviter (Automattic).
- Pre-account takeover: register with a victim's unverified email, enable 2FA or set credentials, lock the real owner out (XVideos).
- 2FA-required-before-invite read from a client-side flag (Omise); 2FA disable without password (Localize); MFA mode value switched to a weaker path (Grammarly).
- Pending invites outliving the inviter (Omise).
- Identity link flows: linking 2FA or a Google login to another account by supplying their identifier (Helium, Shopify POS proxy). Confirmation bypass fixes need a retest for variants (Shopify part II).

# Workflow step skipping and flawed enforcement

Status: SEED
Invariant: a step cannot run unless the prior steps completed, and every step enforces its own authorization.

## Signals
- Multi-step flows (checkout, onboarding, approvals, KYC, invite acceptance, refunds).
- Final step endpoint is callable directly. State lives in the client or a weak token.
- Admin or approval actions exposed to normal users through an API that the UI hides.

## Tests
1. Call the last step first. Call steps out of order. Repeat a completed step.
2. Drop or blank parameters that prove an earlier step (tokens, flags, codes).
3. Switch HTTP method, API version or content type on the sensitive step.
4. Complete the flow in one tenant then replay the final step with another tenant's object id.
5. Approval flows: act as the requester and call the approve endpoint.
6. Sensitive changes (email, phone, 2FA off) without re-authentication or password.

## Distilled variants (from ingested reports)
- State fields writable by the user: on update (PATCH/PUT) endpoints, try the fields the server uses for review and payment state (status, effective_status, admin_approval, approved, verified). Source: H1 1543159 (ad approved and activated without payment or review).
- Client-supplied workflow state: when a request carries a state or step name (for example CREATE_NEW_PASSWORD), send a later state directly without completing the earlier ones. Source: H1 143717.

## Evidence
Final state reached (order placed, status approved, setting changed) with the skipped step shown as not performed.

## Seed reports
H1 1543159 approval and status change without payment details; 783258 2FA disabled without password; 770504 bypass password to update email and phone; 1040047 email verification bypass on signup; 910300 email confirmation bypass leading to privilege escalation.

## State transition abuse (WSTG 10-Business_Logic; distilled)
- Call a later step directly. Reorder steps. Replay an early step after a later one.
- Workflow state inferred from client parameters or spread over several services is the weak spot.
- Credit and points: start a transaction past the point where credits are granted, then cancel or reduce the total, and check whether the credit was reversed.
- Edit saved content into a state the initial validation would have refused (append, edit, remove).

# Access control drill patterns
Status: SEED (original notes from general technique, modelled on the public Web Security Academy topic list; not copied from it)

## Use when
Role-based and object-based access.

## Signals
- Admin paths, ids in requests, role in cookies or parameters.

## Verify safely (bounty-safe: smallest proof, no data dumping, no damage)
Run the matrix: every identity on every route, with and without credentials, and with swapped ids.

## Variants to try
- Unprotected functionality; unpredictable-id leakage; parameter-based role control; role change in profile (mass assignment); URL-based control with override headers; method-based control; multistep process missing a check; referer-based control; horizontal to vertical escalation; insecure direct object references (static files).

## Lab drills (practice pattern: do these on the Academy or a local vulnerable app, never a live target)
- Unprotected admin panel; admin URL from a robots file or script; user role controlled by request parameter; role modification in profile; platform URL-matching bypass; method-based bypass; horizontal escalation; guid leakage; data leakage in redirects; password disclosure in a prefilled field; IDOR on chat logs.

See authz/access-control-test-matrix.md.

files.text:
# Access control test matrix

Status: DISTILLED from Intigriti's BugQuest 2026 access control series and its BAC guide (own words), plus the 2025 and 2026 report batches.
Use after the app model exists. Pick the rows that match the endpoint, test each against two accounts (same role) and one in another tenant.

## Identifier tricks
1. Alias keywords: replace `me`, `my`, `current`, `self` in the path or body with real user, tenant or object ids. Checks often assume users reference only themselves.
2. Parameter pollution: duplicate parameters, arrays, comma-separated lists, URL-encoded ids, wildcards, booleans, null bytes. Validation may read one value while data retrieval reads another.
3. Duplicate JSON keys: send the same key twice in a JSON body. A gateway that validates the first and a backend that reads the last disagree (seen in a 2026 CTF).
4. Path traversal inside an id field when a middleware builds an internal request from it (second-order).

## Verb and format tricks
5. After a 401 or 403 try other methods (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), method override headers, and other Content-Types.
6. Format suffixes: framework URL matching can apply authorization to the HTML route but not to `.json` or `.xml` for the same object.
7. Legacy and parallel paths: `/v1`, `/v2`, `/internal`, mobile API hosts, admin hosts.

## Workflow and second-order
8. Multi-step flows where a later step (archive, transfer, approve) changes ownership or state without re-checking permission.
9. Internal services that trust a shared privileged token, or session variables overwritten by another feature.
10. Lifecycle: invites, shares, tokens and locks that survive revocation (see privilege-escalation).

## Discovery sources for hidden routes
robots.txt, sitemap.xml, swagger or OpenAPI files, .git config, JS bundles and source maps, GraphQL introspection, Postman collections, web archives, code search, mobile apps (unpack, bypass pinning, check API versions).

## Tooling
Parallel sessions per role (browser containers) and an authorization replay extension (Autorize style) to replay every request with each role's token. Feed the diff results into the ledger.

## What triage rejects (so do not report it)
- Swapping your own two accounts and seeing each one's own data.
- Public catalog data returned as JSON or XML.
- Theoretical issues with no exploit path, or ids that cannot realistically be obtained.
- A finding needs demonstrable confidentiality, integrity or availability impact.

## Additions (WSTG 05, Bugcrowd disclosures; distilled)
- Three axes for every function: unauthenticated (forced browsing), horizontal (peer), vertical (higher role). Automate with an endpoint list plus Autorize, ZAP access-control add-on or Burp Intruder.
- Path normalization: encoded or doubled slashes, encoded characters inside a protected prefix, trailing dot or slash can skip the auth layer while the backend still routes to the protected handler. Several NASA disclosures (auth bypass via double slash, encoded path on an SSO key endpoint) follow this shape.
- Verb tampering: the guard covers GET and POST, another verb reaches the same handler unguarded.
- BFLA vs IDOR: a function reachable by a low role (list all requests, manage others) is a separate finding from reading one object by id.
- Provisioning (WSTG 03): who may create or delete accounts, can an admin make a higher privilege than their own, can a user deprovision themselves, what happens to the removed user's data.
- Unauthenticated write: exposed data stores, webhooks and dashboards (Flink, Elasticsearch) are repeated hits on VDP programs; check these on in-scope infra.

## PortSwigger access control types (distilled)
Vertical, horizontal, horizontal to vertical (peer access used to reach an admin's data or reset path), context-dependent (out of sequence or after state should block). Weak spots to test: unlinked admin paths (robots.txt, JS, wordlist); role in a cookie, hidden field or query (admin=true, role=1); front-end URL blocks that honour X-Original-URL or X-Rewrite-URL; case, extension and trailing-slash variants of restricted paths; method swaps; Referer-based checks; geography checks (only where in scope).

# Alternate paths and derived assets
Status: DISTILLED
Trigger: a feature gated well on its main route, but the same data or action is reachable another way.
Source: batch 04 (about 250 reports, rewritten in own words).

## The idea
Authorization is usually written once per route. Hunt for every other route that reaches the same object or action and check each independently.

## Where the second path hides
- UI gate versus API: button disabled for the role, API still accepts it (Dust tables, Lovable workspace toggles, Pontoon pin and unapprove). Replay each gated action with the lowest credential.
- Same action, other endpoint: slash-command execute posting for a user without post right (Mattermost), admin panel email update without current password (Revive), summary report attachment ids (H1).
- Derived assets: a transformation of a private file became public (Mozilla); presigned or preview URLs; cover images and thumbnails; export files.
- Copy, clone, import, template, transfer: project import and template copy moving private issues across projects (GitLab), cloned agent keeping admin power (Dust), account import crossing tenants (Basecamp), federated "add to my cloud" turning read-only into write (Nextcloud).
- Parent versus child ownership: parent campaign checked, child banner not (Revive); tag synonyms by id skipping per-tag rules (Discourse).
- Second id space or older sibling property: legacy site with unprotected DELETE (Reddit gifts), undocumented GraphQL mutation (Shopify fileCopy), launch-day new endpoints missing scope checks (X Fleets).
- Scope level: API key limited to one program reading another in the same organization (H1).
- Hidden by UI only: privacy flags honoured in the app but not by GraphQL, lookups or invite-by-id (hidden likes, private email via invite or leaderboard, discoverability by phone).

## Tests
1. Build a role by object matrix. For each cell find every route that can perform it (web, API, GraphQL, mobile, import, command, integration).
2. Replay with the lowest role and a second tenant.
3. After a copy or derive, check the new object's permissions against the source.
4. Re-read after a failed or partial request; persisted references strengthen evidence.

## Novelty note
Plain id swaps are crowded. Import, clone, derive and integration paths on newly shipped features are where duplicates are rarer.

## Revocation lag (pwnpanda list)
Removing or lowering a role often leaves other things alive: staff whose email was changed or deleted (Shopify partners), preview tokens after app uninstall, sessions after password change (Moneybird), invites after the inviter is removed (Omise). After any role change, test the old session, old tokens, preview links and pending invites.

## Later modules and locked states (New Relic, Visma series)
- Products grown in layers: the older modules enforce the role model, newer ones (Synthetics, NerdGraph, a swapped billing vendor, test or preview endpoints) often skip it. Walk every module as the lowest role and call endpoints directly.
- Locked states (archived company, read-only, expired session, restricted role) frequently lock only the UI: replay delete and update calls, and open data pages by URL.
- Test, preview and debug endpoints for a feature often validate neither ownership nor permission.

# Function level authorization (BFLA) and forged claims
Status: SEED

Trigger: admin, staff, approval or management routes, or any role claim in a token or request body.

1. List every admin-looking route from recon, JS and docs: `/admin/`, `/manage`, `/internal`, `approve`, `delete_`, `toggle`, `create_admin`, `suspend`, `export`.
2. For each, send it as: no auth, normal user, and (if you hold one) the admin account. Record status and body for all three. A 200 or any state change as the normal user is the finding; a 403 is the control.
3. Do the verb swap: GET vs POST vs PUT vs DELETE on the same path. Do the format swap: `/admin/x`, `/ADMIN/x`, `/admin/x/`, `/api/v1` vs `/api/v2` copies.
4. Client claims: if the token or body carries `is_admin` or `role`, test body parameters on register, profile update and login (`is_admin:true`, `role:"admin"`, `balance`). Compare the response with a plain call.
5. Second-order: an admin list page that renders data you control (username, bio, description) is a stored XSS target for admin sessions. Note it, test with a harmless marker only.

Chain value: BFLA plus an info leak that discloses admin credentials or tokens is often critical. Record both findings, then chain.

files.text:
# File and document access control
Status: SEED

## Use when
Download links, statements, invoices, KYC documents, attachments, chat media, report exports, avatars, backups, user-uploaded files.

## Tests
- Predictable names: sequential ids, user id plus date, hash of a guessable value. Request another account's file by changing the id (your own second account).
- Unauthenticated access: copy the file URL to a private window; open it without cookies. Files behind a "private" app often serve from a CDN or storage host with no check.
- Signed URLs: long expiry, reuse after logout, signature not bound to the user, parameters changeable (`file=` swapped keeping `sig=`), signature algorithm none or empty.
- Path parameters: `?file=../..` (see `server-side/path-traversal.md`), file ids mapped to storage keys directly.
- Derived files: thumbnails, previews, resized images, PDF exports and ZIP bundles that bypass the permission check of the original.
- Delete and replace: another user's attachment replaced or deleted (write BOLA).
- Search indexes and autocompletes returning titles of private documents.
- Version history and trash: deleted files still accessible by id.
- Content type and headers: user uploads served inline from the main origin (XSS), missing `nosniff`, `Content-Disposition` absent.

## Evidence
Two own accounts, one file of each, the request to the other's file with status and size. Do not download others' real documents; confirm with your own test files.

# GraphQL authorization

Status: SEED
Invariant: each resolver and field enforces access, not just the top-level query.

## Signals
- /graphql endpoint, introspection enabled, persisted queries in JS, nested types with user fields (email, phone, private lists).

## Tests
1. Pull the schema (introspection or from JS persisted queries). List every field that returns user or private data.
2. Query nested paths to sensitive fields through objects you may legitimately reach (invitation to user to email).
3. Mutations with another user's ids, as in idor-bola.
4. Aliases and batching to bypass rate limits on brute force checks.
5. Compare web, mobile and partner GraphQL endpoints; policies often differ.

## Distilled variants (from ingested reports)
- Mutation responses leak data: a mutation that adds a participant by username returned the invitation object with the user's email (H1 792927). Request every field of every mutation payload type, not just the success flag.
- Bulk id arguments: a delete mutation taking a list of ids had no ownership check, and the ids of public posts appear in share URLs (H1 1819832).

## Evidence
Field value that your role should not see, returned for an object or user you own.

## Seed reports
H1 792927 email of any user via a nested invitation type; 885539 private list members disclosure; 2122671 delete data via GraphQL mutation with another user's id.

## Enumeration and batching (PayloadsAllTheThings; distilled)
- Find the endpoint (/graphql, /api/graphql, /graphiql, /v1/graphql). Try introspection; if blocked, use field-suggestion errors to rebuild the schema, and look for paths to a sensitive type from reachable types.
- Arguments on fields are the IDOR entry points; walk nested relations (user to posts to comments) because authorization is often checked only at the root.
- Mutations: test each reference argument with another tenant's id (see tenant-isolation).
- Batching and aliases: many operations in one request bypass per-request rate limits (login, OTP, coupon) and trigger simultaneous writes for races.

## Black-box GraphQL checklist (added v1.4)
1. Introspection: POST `{"query":"{__schema{types{name fields{name}}}}"}`. Enabled in production = finding (informational to low) and gives you the full operation list. Control: a query for a field that does not exist returns the normal error.
2. Auth: call each query and mutation with no token, a normal user, and an admin if you hold one. Admin-scoped analytics reachable by a normal user is BFLA.
3. Object arguments: swap ids and account numbers across accounts (see `authz/idor-bola.md`).
4. Injection: string arguments that end up in a SQL query. Use the quote and boolean pair from `injection/sqli-safe-verification.md` inside the argument value.
5. Depth and complexity: one nested query a few levels deep and one batched array of 5 operations, to see whether limits exist. Do not flood.
6. Errors: malformed queries that return stack traces or SQL text.


## From real reports
Top-voted disclosed reports for this class: `knowledge-base/training/reports/graphql.md`; patterns in own words: `training/report-patterns.md` (section graphql); search all 16,024 in the Library Reports tab.

files.text:
# IDOR and object-level authorization

Status: SEED
Invariant: every object access checks ownership or permission on the server, for every method and route.

## Signals
- IDs in path, query, body, headers, GraphQL arguments, cookies, JWT claims.
- Several routes touch the same object (v1 and v2, mobile and web, export, share, webhook).

## Tests
1. Two accounts, same role: replay A's request with B's object id, for GET, PUT, PATCH, DELETE.
2. Find other routes for the same object (export, print, preview, download, attachment, comment, history).
3. Unpredictable ids are not a defense: find where ids leak (lists, emails, errors, JS, shared links).
4. Parameter pollution, array of ids, wildcard or negative ids, id in a different case or type.
5. Check side effects: changing email or phone on another user leads to account takeover.
6. Check write and delete separately; they are often less protected than read.

## Distilled variants (2025 and 2026 reports)
- Destructive endpoint trusts a body identity: account destroy took the victim email (and a password hash) from the JSON body and ignored the session. If the first version needs a victim secret, test accounts that have no password set (SSO only), where an email alone may be enough. Triage rejected the first version; the second was rated High. Source: H1 3154983.
- Two-object features: compare, diff, merge, copy, fork, import, template. Give the second reference to an object you cannot read (known name, branch or SHA). Source: H1 3124517 (GitHub Enterprise compare leaked private repo code).
- Error bodies leak: a 422 or 403 on an object endpoint still returned the object's subject and details in the body. Always read the full body of denied responses. Source: H1 3862641.

## Distilled variants (batch 03)
- Other access paths for the same data: access control enforced by a query filter or UI layer but not by the single-item REST route, export, feed, preview or attachment URL. Test the collection and the single item separately (H1 3801107, WordPress bbPress).
- Path user vs session user: URLs or DAV paths carrying a user id that the server does not compare with the session (H1 3301553, 3382343).
- CRM portals (Salesforce style): predictable record ids plus custom controller actions such as clone or link; test ownership on each action (H1 2950536).
- Global incrementing ids across accounts make cross-account guessing trivial; look for a shared counter (H1 3979217).
- Reality check: plain numeric-id IDOR on a simple GET is high volume and often a duplicate or informative (H1 3259610, 3382343 closed informative). Prefer the variants above.

## Evidence
Another user's object (your own second account) read or changed, control request showing correct denial elsewhere.

## Seed reports
H1 415081 add users to a business account; 1819832 delete anyone's content; 751577 payments data of any user; 876300 account takeover via IDOR; 380410 delete other users' photos; 1969141 and 2122671 delete data by id in GraphQL and REST; 3862641 report details via secondary endpoint; 2442008 attachment disclosure through a summary route.

## Bugcrowd examples (distilled)
Unauthenticated read, create and delete of any user's data on an app with only a user id; UUID-based file references that still lacked an access check (UUID is not authorization); IDOR returning profile and PII; IDOR that exposed credentials of another district's users and let the tester attach themselves as parent to any student (write plus read in one flaw). Check write and relationship-creating endpoints, not just reads.

## Identifier tricks (PayloadsAllTheThings; distilled)
- Sequential decimal, hex, or epoch-timestamp ids: step up and down.
- Guessable ids: usernames, emails, base64 of them.
- Predictable generators: UUID v1 (time based), MongoDB ObjectIds (timestamp, machine, process, counter), so one known id narrows the neighbours.
- Hashed ids such as md5(email) or sha1(username): compute them for a target you know.
- Wildcard values (`*`, `%`, `null`, `0`, `-1`) and arrays of ids in one request.
- Confirmed shapes from public reports: view orders, delete messages or campaigns, read another user's token on an ads service.

files.text:
# Multi-role testing workflow (PwnFox, Autorize, Auth Analyzer)
Status: DISTILLED
Trigger: any app with two or more roles or tenants. Use before manual IDOR hunting to shortlist, never as proof.

## Setup
1. Create at least two accounts per role you can get (admin, member, read-only) plus one in a second tenant.
2. Keep each in its own browser container (PwnFox colours requests per role in Burp history).
3. Define scope first so only in-scope traffic is replayed.

## Run
- Autorize: paste the low-privilege session; browse as the high-privilege user; it replays each request with the low session and with none. Red means possibly bypassed, orange needs a check, green likely enforced.
- Auth Analyzer: one session per user (cookies and auth headers), browse as the privileged user, add parameter rules for rotating CSRF tokens or values pulled from responses, use replay-login mode to keep sessions alive in long runs, diff view for candidates. For CORS checks replace the Origin header and drop OPTIONS.
- Exercise every feature and every method (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) as the privileged user, creating, editing and deleting, since coverage decides what gets tested.

## Verify (mandatory)
Compare original, modified and unauthenticated response lengths; open the replayed response and confirm it holds the other account's data, not an error page; resend by hand in Repeater; then run the novelty filter.

## Gap
These tools replay requests but do not know your business rules. Add the invariant list from the hypotheses stage and test state-dependent cases by hand.

files.text:
# Role and privilege escalation

Status: SEED
Invariant: each action requires the right role on every route, and a user cannot grant themselves or others more than they hold.

## Signals
- Role or permission fields in requests, admin pages hidden in the UI, invite flows with roles, owner/admin/member tiers.

## Tests
1. Call admin or manager endpoints with a member token (found in JS, docs, or traffic of an admin account you own).
2. Mass assignment: add role, is_admin, permissions, owner_id to profile or invite requests.
3. Change your own role through the team member update route; change someone else's above your level.
4. Access list or group owners escalating to higher roles by editing the list.
5. Path and method tricks on admin routes (case, trailing slash, method override, redirect without stopping).
6. Embedded or partner submission forms that skip role checks or 2FA requirements.

## Distilled variants (from ingested reports)
- Delegated ownership: an owner of a group or list may manage members but not the roles the list grants. Add a member while setting the grants field in the same request and see whether the server accepts it (H1 2281075). Read the product docs for rules like this and test each one.
- Email verification bound to the account instead of the address: confirm an address in one state, then switch the pending address, so a mailbox you do not control ends up verified. That can enable SSO or federated identity setup and takeover (H1 910300). Test change-email followed by confirm with the address swapped between steps.

## Distilled variants (2025 and 2026 reports, batch 03)
- Lowest-role replay: for every role in the app model, replay each admin-only route as the lowest role. A Builder role could list, create and silently overwrite workspace secrets by reusing a name (H1 3103755). Conversation routes in a workspace had no per-object check on GET, PATCH and DELETE (H1 3103849).
- Delegated or partial admins (API-only, group-scoped): test whether they can touch objects outside their scope by sequential id, for example adding their own group to every Team Folder (H1 3674940).
- Sibling endpoints: diff checks between a core route and its wrapper, or between report classes in the same plugin. An AND where OR was needed, or a permission callback that always returns true, are typical (H1 3871816, 4029867).
- Verb differences: write handlers authorized on a weaker rule than read handlers. With your own account id in the path and the victim's object id, PUT and DELETE worked while GET returned 403 (H1 3979217). Test every verb separately and every host that serves the API.
- Lifecycle: what survives share revocation, role removal and account deletion (locks, tokens, webhooks, approvals) (H1 3770482).
- Optional guard parameters: remove parameters that guard a check (etag, version, token). The check ran only when the parameter was present (H1 3610332).

## Distilled variants (batch 04)
- Invite stores an unvalidated role: the UI dropdown hides roles, but the request carries role and the server persists it before checking editable roles, so an Editor invited a user as Administrator (H1 3942522). Also test invite role on accept.
- Invite and membership lifecycle: pending invites and members added by an admin stay valid after that admin is removed (H1 3303136). Test removal of the inviter, role downgrade, and invite expiry.
- Hidden objects reached by id paths: a tag you cannot view could be mutated by submitting its numeric id in a synonym or settings request; authorization covered only the visible target (H1 3689633). Test every request that accepts a list of ids.
- Vertical actions on moderation routes (unapprove, pin, delete) that check login but not role (H1 3020021, 3025797).
- Payment binding: payment confirmation not bound to the order (no stored payment request id or amount), fail-open signature checks, and a token from the query string outside the signed body (H1 3941626). Compare against the sibling payment method in the same plugin.

## Evidence
Action only a higher role should do, performed with a lower role you own.

## Seed reports
H1 605720 program permission escalates to admin; 2281075 access list owner escalates role; 418767 bypass 2FA requirement through embedded form; 683957 admin authentication bypass by stopping the redirect; 270981 admin authentication bypass via partner site.

## Mass assignment (PayloadsAllTheThings, OWASP; distilled)
ORMs that bind the whole body to an object accept fields the UI never sends (isAdmin, role, plan, verified, ownerId, tenantId). Test: read the object's full JSON from a GET, then PUT or PATCH it back with the privileged fields changed, and also add guessed names. Try on signup, profile update, invite accept and resource create. Check the change persists and takes effect, not only that the response echoes it.
