files.text:
# Shadow, old and undocumented APIs
Status: SEED

## Use when
Any API, especially after a redesign or a mobile release cycle. Old versions keep working long after the new one gets its security fixes.

## Find them
- Version in path (`/v1/`, `/v2/`), subdomain (`api-v1`, `api-old`, `legacy`), header (`Accept: application/vnd.x.v1+json`, `X-API-Version`), query (`?version=1`).
- From the front end: JS bundles, source maps, mobile app strings, old app versions, Wayback captures, public docs for old versions, Postman collections, GitHub repositories of the company.
- Internal-looking hosts: `internal`, `admin`, `dev`, `staging`, `uat`, `test`, `sandbox`, `beta`, `partner`, `b2b`, `gateway`. Remember scope: test only hosts the program covers.
- Documentation endpoints: `/swagger`, `/swagger.json`, `/openapi.json`, `/api-docs`, `/v3/api-docs`, `/docs`, `/redoc`, `/graphql` with introspection, `/.well-known/`. See `api/openapi-and-documentation-exposure.md`.
- Framework defaults: Spring `/actuator/*`, ASP.NET `/elmah.axd`, `/trace.axd`, Django `/admin`, Laravel `/telescope`, `/horizon`, Rails `/rails/info`.

## Test
Take each request that is protected on the current version and send it to the old version with the same token and with another user's ids. Compare: missing authorization, missing rate limit, missing field filtering, different error verbosity.

## Report
Show the old and new request side by side with the control. The fix is retiring the old version or applying the same checks in a shared layer.

files.text:
# SOAP, WSDL, gRPC, JSON-RPC and other RPC services
Status: SEED

## Use when
Bank and enterprise back ends often expose SOAP (`?wsdl`, `.asmx`, `.svc`), JSON-RPC, gRPC, XML-RPC or custom binary protocols.

## SOAP and WSDL
- Fetch `?wsdl` and `?singleWsdl`: every operation and type is listed, including admin operations the UI never calls. Build requests for each and test with no auth and a low-privilege account.
- WS-Security headers: missing signature validation, username tokens in plaintext over HTTP.
- XML parser flaws: external entities (`server-side/xxe.md`), XML injection into fields that become part of the next message, XPath in lookups (`injection/other-injection-classes.md`), SOAPAction header ignored and replaced.
- Verbose faults: stack traces, internal host names, database errors.

## JSON-RPC and XML-RPC
`system.listMethods` (XML-RPC) and `rpc.discover` (OpenRPC) list methods. Batch requests multiply cost and can bypass rate limits; `system.multicall` allows many attempts in one request (brute force).

## gRPC and protobuf
- Reflection enabled on production (`grpcurl list`) exposes the service schema. Call each method with and without credentials; authorization is often only implemented on some methods.
- Metadata (headers) as identity: `x-user-id` accepted from the client.
- gRPC-web endpoints reachable through the browser path; proxies that translate may skip authentication.

## Message queues and brokers
Exposed brokers (RabbitMQ management on 15672 with default credentials only if testing is allowed, Kafka without authentication, MQTT topics `#` subscribe). Read topic names only to prove exposure.

## Report
The operation or method list as exposure evidence, and one unauthenticated or unauthorized call with its result.

files.text:
# Webhooks and callbacks
Status: SEED

## Use when
The app sends or receives webhooks, payment notifications, callbacks, or lets users register callback URLs.

## Receiving side (your target receives webhooks)
- Is the signature verified? Send the callback with no signature, a wrong one, and a valid one for another payload. If a payment "success" callback is accepted without a verifiable signature, an attacker can mark orders paid.
- Replay: send the same valid callback twice. Duplicate credit means no idempotency.
- Amount and currency in the callback versus the order: do they match? Do they use the callback amount or the stored order amount?
- Source IP allowlist only, with spoofable headers (`X-Forwarded-For`).
- Callback ordering: "failed" arriving after "success".

## Sending side (the target calls URLs you register)
- SSRF: register an internal address, a metadata address or a name you control that resolves to one. Use your own listener and harmless targets, stay inside scope. See `server-side/ssrf.md` and `cloud/cloud-metadata-and-ssrf.md`.
- Redirect following into internal addresses; DNS rebinding; non-HTTP schemes.
- Secrets sent in webhook bodies or headers to user-chosen URLs.
- Webhook management authorization: can you list, edit or delete another tenant's webhooks (BOLA)? Can you read their secrets?
- Verbose delivery logs exposing response bodies from internal systems.

## Proof
Your own callback listener receiving the request, with headers and time; or the accepted unsigned callback and the changed order status on your own order.

files.text:
# Android app testing
Status: SEED

## Use when
The target has an Android app (APK), or the web app has a mobile API that only the app talks to. The app is often the weakest door: it holds keys, hidden endpoints and older API versions.

## Set up (own device or emulator, own test accounts)
1. Get the APK from the store or the client. Unpack it (`apktool d`, `jadx`) and read, do not run yet.
2. Route traffic through your proxy. If the app refuses (certificate pinning), see `mobile/mobile-api-and-certificate-pinning.md`.

## Static review: what to look for
- `AndroidManifest.xml`: `android:exported="true"` activities, services, receivers and providers without a permission; `android:debuggable="true"`; `android:allowBackup="true"` (adb backup of app data); `usesCleartextTraffic="true"`; custom URL schemes and intent filters (see `mobile/deep-links-and-webviews.md`).
- Strings and resources: API base URLs (staging, test, internal), API keys, client secrets, Firebase URLs and `google-services.json`, AWS keys, hardcoded tokens, basic-auth strings, private keys, feature flags. A key found here is a lead; prove it with one harmless call and report the exposure, not the data behind it.
- Hidden endpoints: every URL in the code that the UI never calls. Admin, debug, v1 and beta routes are common.
- Crypto: hardcoded AES keys or IVs, ECB mode, MD5 or SHA1 for passwords, `Math.random`/`java.util.Random` for tokens, custom "encryption" of requests.
- Local auth: biometric or PIN checks done only on the client (a boolean in the app decides), root detection that only hides a message.

## Dynamic review
- Local storage after login and logout: `shared_prefs`, SQLite databases, files, cache, WebView storage. Tokens, PINs, card numbers, full profile data in plaintext are findings; tokens still present after logout are a session finding.
- Logs (`adb logcat`) and clipboard: tokens, OTP codes, request bodies in logs.
- Screenshots and recent-apps preview of screens with balances or card data (`FLAG_SECURE` missing). Low severity unless the program values it.
- Exported components: call them with `adb shell am start` or a small test app using your own account. Prove an unauthenticated screen or data leak, nothing more.
- Server side is the real target: every request the app makes should be replayed with another account's ids (BOLA), with a missing token, with an older app version header, and with changed amounts.

## Reporting
Show the manifest line or the stored file, the exact path on the device, and what an attacker with the device (or malware with no permissions) can reach. Rate by data type: session tokens and PINs matter more than a cached avatar.

files.text:
# Deep links, intents and WebViews
Status: SEED

## Use when
The app registers URL schemes (`myapp://`), app links (`https://app.example.com/path` opening the app), exported Android components, or shows web content inside a WebView.

## Deep links
- Find them: manifest intent filters (Android), `CFBundleURLTypes` and associated domains (iOS), plus links the web app generates.
- Test: open each link with parameters you control. Can a link make the app perform an action without a confirmation (transfer, change email, logout, add beneficiary)? Can it load a URL you choose inside the app? Can it carry a token or code in the URL that another app can intercept (custom schemes can be claimed by other apps; verified app links cannot)?
- OAuth redirects to a custom scheme are interceptable by a malicious app on the same device unless PKCE is used. Check for PKCE.
- Check the digital asset links file (`/.well-known/assetlinks.json`, `apple-app-site-association`): wrong or wildcard entries.

## WebViews
- `setJavaScriptEnabled(true)` plus `addJavascriptInterface` exposes native methods to any page loaded. If the WebView can load an attacker-chosen URL (through a deep link parameter or an open redirect on a trusted host), page script can call those methods.
- `setAllowFileAccess`, `setAllowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs`: local file reads from web content.
- Loading HTTP content, ignoring TLS errors (`onReceivedSslError` calling `proceed`).
- Session cookies shared between WebView and app; tokens placed in the URL query.
- iOS: `WKWebView` with `javaScriptEnabled` and message handlers; `UIWebView` is old and risky.

## Exported components (Android)
Activities, services, receivers and providers with `exported=true` and no permission can be called by any app. Content providers with path traversal or SQL injection in the selection arguments are classic. Prove with your own test app that reads only your own test account's data.

## Proof and rating
A deep link that performs a sensitive action without confirmation, from a web page the user visits, is the strongest form (High). A reachable but harmless screen is informational.

files.text:
# Dynamic mobile analysis workflow
Status: SEED

## Use when
Static review is done and you want to see what the app really sends: tokens, PII, cleartext, pinning, trackers.

## Steps (own emulator or test phone, own test account)
1. Proxy the device through mitmproxy running the Invariant capture add-on.
2. First run WITHOUT SSL hooks. If API traffic appears, the app does not pin: that is the finding.
3. If it fails, run again with the Frida SSL, root and storage scripts, and tell Invariant the hooks were active.
4. Walk every screen, then upload the capture. Invariant flags cleartext, secrets in URLs, PII in responses, auth over HTTP, third-party hosts.
5. Test the backend hosts with permission; capture findings are leads, not proof.

## Limits
Invariant does not drive the phone. iOS needs a jailbroken device for Frida. Untested on real devices here.

files.text:
# iOS app testing
Status: SEED

## Use when
The target has an iOS app (IPA). Same server-side checks as Android, different local storage and platform features.

## Static review
- Unzip the IPA. Read `Info.plist`: `NSAppTransportSecurity` exceptions (`NSAllowsArbitraryLoads`, per-domain exceptions to HTTP), `CFBundleURLTypes` (custom schemes), `LSApplicationQueriesSchemes`, associated domains (`applinks:` entries show the web hosts that open the app).
- Strings in the binary and bundled files: API URLs, keys, plist secrets, `GoogleService-Info.plist`, embedded certificates, `.p12` files with passwords.
- Frameworks: old third-party SDKs with known CVEs (version match is a lead).

## Dynamic review (own device, own accounts)
- Keychain: items stored with `kSecAttrAccessibleAlways` or without access control hold tokens that survive reinstall and are readable on a jailbroken device. Check what is in Keychain after logout.
- Files: `NSUserDefaults`, plist files, SQLite, Core Data, cache and snapshots in the app container. Tokens, PINs, PAN, full statements in plaintext.
- Pasteboard: sensitive fields that allow copy, general pasteboard use for OTP or card numbers.
- Backgrounding: app snapshot showing balances (no blur or privacy screen).
- URL schemes and universal links: another app or a web page can open the app with parameters. See `mobile/deep-links-and-webviews.md`.
- Jailbreak detection and pinning: bypassing them is a test step, not a finding. The finding is what the server accepts once traffic is visible.

## Server side
Same list as Android: BOLA with other ids, missing token, old app versions, amount tampering, race on transfers, rate limits on login and OTP.

## Reporting
Evidence is the file or Keychain entry and the realistic attacker (lost device, malware, shared device). State the platform setting that would fix it.

files.text:
# Mobile API testing and certificate pinning
Status: SEED

## Use when
The app talks to an API you cannot see through the normal proxy, or the API accepts only requests that look like the app.

## Seeing the traffic (own device, authorized scope)
1. Install your proxy CA on the test device. On modern Android the user CA is ignored by apps unless they opt in, so use an emulator with a rooted image or a patched debug build when the client allows it.
2. If pinning blocks you, the options in order of cheapness: the client provides a build without pinning; a dynamic instrumentation script on your own device; patching the pin check in the unpacked app. Pinning bypass is a method, not a finding.
3. If the app uses a non-HTTP protocol (gRPC, MQTT, websockets, custom TCP), capture with a packet tool and decode with the schema from the app.

## What mobile APIs often get wrong
- Authorization only in the app: hidden fields in the UI are not security. Every action must be re-checked on the server with the account and object ids.
- Older versions: `/api/v1/` stays alive after `/api/v3/` ships, without the new checks. Send old versions and old `User-Agent` or `X-App-Version` values.
- Device binding: tokens that work on any device, device ids the client chooses, "trusted device" flags the client sends.
- Request signing: signatures made with a key inside the app. Extract the key, then the signature does not protect anything. Check whether the server verifies the signature at all by changing a field and keeping the old one.
- Static API keys per app, shared by all users, with powers beyond the app's needs.
- Verbose errors and debug endpoints (`/debug`, `/actuator`, `/swagger`) that the web app hides.
- Push and OTP: OTP returned in the response, OTP reused across devices, no rate limit on OTP requests (SMS cost abuse; report it as a limit gap, send to your own number only).
- Rate limits keyed on device id or IP header the client controls.

## Proof
Replay the exact app request with your own second account's object id and a changed field. Keep the request, the response and the control with your own object.

files.text:
# Mobile local storage and embedded secrets
Status: SEED

## Use when
Any mobile app. Quick pass that finds the most common reportable items on a client-provided device.

## Checklist (Android and iOS)
1. After login, list the app's files and databases. Search them for the account's token, email, phone, PAN, PIN, passwords, OTP seeds.
2. Log out. List again. Anything left that still authorizes API calls is a session finding; copy the token and call the API with it.
3. Uninstall and reinstall: iOS Keychain items survive. Tokens that survive and still work are a finding.
4. Search the package for secrets: cloud keys (`AKIA`, `AIza`), private keys (`BEGIN PRIVATE KEY`), Firebase and Stripe or payment keys, client secrets, JWT signing secrets, basic auth, database strings. Separate public keys (publishable, restricted) from secret keys.
5. Check what a found key can do with one harmless read call. Do not enumerate data behind it.
6. Third-party SDK keys: analytics, maps, push. Usually low unless the key is unrestricted and costs money (maps keys: restrict by app or referrer).
7. Backups: Android `allowBackup`, iOS unencrypted iTunes backups include app data.
8. Biometric gate: bypassable if the secret sits in the app next to the check, not protected by the OS keystore.

## Severity guide
Secret key with write power or admin: Critical. Token or PAN in plaintext on the device: Medium to High depending on program (needs device access). Public client key: Info. State the attacker precondition honestly.

files.title: Mobile app static review with a second reviewer
files.text:
# Mobile app static review with a second reviewer

Status: SEED
Invariant: a finding one tool sees alone is a hint; a finding two independent readers agree on is a result.

## Use when
You hold an APK or IPA for an in-scope app, or a web target links to one, and want the backend hosts, exposed components and stored secrets.

## Android
Check: debuggable, allowBackup, cleartext traffic and network security config, user CA trust, minSdk, signing scheme (v2/v3), exported activities, services, receivers and providers without a permission, custom URL schemes and unverified web links, key-shaped strings in DEX, resources and bundled assets, React Native or Cordova bundles (run the JavaScript analysis on them), bundled key stores and databases.

## iOS
Check: App Transport Security exceptions, get-task-allow and push environment in the provisioning profile, URL schemes, associated domains, the executable's strings, bundled JavaScript, privacy usage keys. Binary hardening flags need a second tool.

## Two reviewers
Reviewer one: the built-in analyzer. Reviewer two: MobSF (REST API) and, for Android manifests, an independent parser. Agreement on the same issue key makes it confirmed and restores its severity. One reviewer alone is capped at low and labelled unconfirmed. Never raise severity because a list looks short.

## After the review
Backend hosts are leads: confirm who owns each before testing; third-party hosts need the owner's permission. Firebase and bucket names are leads to test only if in scope. A client key meant to be public (map keys) is not a flaw until you show what it unlocks.

files.text:
# Clickjacking
Status: SEED (original notes from general technique, modelled on the public Web Security Academy topic list; not copied from it)

## Use when
Sensitive one-click actions on pages that can be framed.

## Signals
- No `X-Frame-Options` and no CSP `frame-ancestors` on an action page.

## Verify safely (bounty-safe: smallest proof, no data dumping, no damage)
1. Check framing headers on the sensitive page.
2. Build a frame page where your test account's real button sits under a decoy; show the action completes.

## Variants to try
- Pre-filled forms from query parameters; frame busters bypassed with sandbox attributes; combined with DOM XSS; multistep actions.

## Lab drills (practice pattern: do these on the Academy or a local vulnerable app, never a live target)
- Basic; with pre-filled form; frame buster bypass; combined with DOM XSS; multistep.

## Triage notes
Many programs reject clickjacking on pages with no sensitive action. Show a real state change.

## Lab catalogue

files.text:
# Cross-origin resource sharing misconfiguration
Status: SEED (original notes from general technique, modelled on the public Web Security Academy topic list; not copied from it)

## Use when
APIs that send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` with credentials.

## Signals
- Response reflects an arbitrary origin, allows `null`, or trusts sub-domains and suffixes; `Allow-Credentials: true`.

## Verify safely (bounty-safe: smallest proof, no data dumping, no damage)
1. Send an `Origin` header with a controlled value, with `null`, with a sibling-domain and a suffix look-alike; see what is reflected and whether credentials are allowed.
2. Prove with a page on your own origin that reads an authenticated, sensitive response for your test account.

## Variants to try
- Reflected origin; `null` origin via sandboxed iframe; regex mistakes (`example.com.evil.com`, `evilexample.com`); trusted subdomain plus XSS there; HTTPS app trusting HTTP origin; internal network trust.
- Without credentials the issue is usually informational.

## Lab drills (practice pattern: do these on the Academy or a local vulnerable app, never a live target)
- Basic origin reflection; trusted null; trusted insecure protocol; intranet pivot.

## Triage notes
A reflecting policy on an endpoint with no sensitive data is low. Show a cross-origin read of private data.

## Lab catalogue
3 Academy labs for this topic with levels, entry points and payload starting points: `training/academy/cross-origin-resource-sharing-cors.md`

# Cross-site request forgery
Status: SEED (original notes from general technique, modelled on the public Web Security Academy topic list; not copied from it)

## Use when
State-changing requests relying on cookies for authentication.

## Signals
- No anti-CSRF token, token not tied to the session, token only checked when present, or SameSite not set and `Lax+POST` window exists.

## Verify safely (bounty-safe: smallest proof, no data dumping, no damage)
1. Identify a state-changing request that uses cookies only.
2. Remove the token, use another user's token, switch method, remove the referer; check what still works.
3. Build a harmless proof of concept page that changes a field on your own test account.

## Variants to try
- Token not validated; token validated only for POST; token tied to a non-session cookie; token duplicated in a cookie; referer check bypass (missing header, suffix match); SameSite bypass (method override, `Lax` after two minutes, sibling-domain gadgets, client-side redirect).
- JSON bodies with `text/plain` content type; GET that changes state.
- Login CSRF and logout CSRF are usually low.

## Lab drills (practice pattern: do these on the Academy or a local vulnerable app, never a live target)
- No defenses; token validation depends on method; depends on presence; not tied to the session; tied to a non-session cookie; token duplicated in cookie; referer validation depends on header; referer validation broken; SameSite Strict and Lax bypasses.

## Triage notes
Show a state change that matters (email change, funds, role). Logout CSRF and similar are normally rejected.

## Lab catalogue

files.text:
# DOM-based vulnerabilities
Status: SEED (original notes from general technique, modelled on the public Web Security Academy topic list; not copied from it)

## Use when
JavaScript reads attacker-controlled sources (`location`, `document.referrer`, `window.name`, `postMessage`, web storage, fragments) and writes them to sinks.

## Signals
- Client code uses `innerHTML`, `document.write`, `eval`, `setTimeout(string)`, `location =`, jQuery `$()` selectors with input, or message handlers without origin checks.

## Verify safely (bounty-safe: smallest proof, no data dumping, no damage)
1. Grep the bundles for sources and sinks; trace one path by hand.
2. Use a marker in the fragment or `window.name`, confirm it reaches the sink in the browser.
3. Prove with a harmless payload on the same origin.

## Variants to try
- Open redirect via `location`; cookie manipulation; JavaScript injection; document domain; WebSocket URL poisoning; link manipulation; Web message with wildcard origin; DOM clobbering of global names; prototype pollution as a source.
- Taint tools help, but confirm by hand.

## Lab drills (practice pattern: do these on the Academy or a local vulnerable app, never a live target)
- `document.write` with `location.search`; `innerHTML` with `location.search`; jQuery `href` sink; `postMessage` to `innerHTML`; message handler that evaluates JSON; DOM clobbering to defeat a check.

## Triage notes
Report with the exact source, sink and a link that triggers it. Browser support matters: say which browser you used.

## Lab catalogue

# postMessage and cross-window trust
Status: SEED

## Use when
Pages with iframes, popups, OAuth popups, payment widgets, chat widgets, embedded dashboards; JS containing `addEventListener('message'`, `postMessage(`.

## Tests
- Listeners: does the handler check `event.origin` against an exact value? Patterns like `indexOf`, `endsWith('.example.com')`, `startsWith` or no check at all can be bypassed with an attacker-controlled host (`example.com.evil.example`).
- Message content used in dangerous sinks: `innerHTML`, `eval`, `location`, `document.write`, script `src`, jQuery selectors. Send crafted messages from a page you control that frames or opens the target.
- Senders: `postMessage(data, '*')` with sensitive data (tokens, user info) lets any framing page receive it. Open the target in your own page and listen.
- Token handoff: OAuth or payment popups returning tokens via postMessage to a wildcard origin.
- Window references: `window.opener` access after cross-origin navigation (reverse tabnabbing), `target=_blank` links without `rel=noopener` on sensitive pages.

## Report
A short proof-of-concept page on your own origin, the message sent or received, the sink, and what it yields (DOM XSS, token theft). Keep the PoC harmless.

# Single-page apps and JavaScript bundle review
Status: SEED

## Use when
React, Vue, Angular, Svelte front ends. The bundle is a map of the whole product, including routes the user never sees.

## Review steps
1. Download every JS chunk (the main bundle and lazy chunks listed in the manifest or `asset-manifest.json`) and source maps if served (`*.js.map`). A source map in production gives original source and comments.
2. Extract routes: client-side route tables show admin and role-gated pages. Role checks in the client are not security: call the API behind each route as a low-privilege user.
3. Extract API calls and base URLs (staging, internal, third-party), hardcoded tokens and keys, feature flags (`isAdmin`, `betaFeatures`) and flag providers that expose all flags to the client.
4. Look for secrets with context: client keys for maps and analytics are public by design; keys for payment secrets, storage admin, JWT signing, SMTP and database are not.
5. Dangerous sinks: `innerHTML`, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `v-html`, `bypassSecurityTrust*` with user data; `eval`, `new Function`; URL building with unvalidated redirects.
6. State in storage: tokens in `localStorage` (readable by any XSS), user objects with sensitive fields, role claims the UI trusts.
7. Auth glue: refresh token handling, token in URL fragments, postMessage (see `client-side/postmessage-and-cross-window.md`), CORS needs.
8. Third-party scripts: analytics, tag managers, chat widgets on login and payment pages (supply chain risk).
9. Version fingerprinting: framework and library versions for known vulnerabilities (as leads).
10. GraphQL operations in the bundle: all queries and mutations the client uses, plus fragments revealing field names for introspection-off targets.

## Report
Path to the file, the extracted item, and the request that proves it matters (for example the admin API route called with a normal user token).

# WebSocket vulnerabilities
Status: SEED (original notes from general technique, modelled on the public Web Security Academy topic list; not copied from it)

## Use when
Chat, notifications, live data, dashboards using WebSockets.

## Signals
- Upgrade request without a CSRF token or origin check; messages carry user ids or html.

## Verify safely (bounty-safe: smallest proof, no data dumping, no damage)
1. Replay and edit messages with the same rules as HTTP: other users' ids, injected markup, privileged commands.
2. Check the handshake: cookie-only authentication and no origin validation means cross-site hijacking.

## Variants to try
- Message manipulation (XSS, SQLi, XXE through messages); handshake manipulation (IP-based bans, header trust); cross-site WebSocket hijacking from a hostile page; missing authorization per message.

## Lab drills (practice pattern: do these on the Academy or a local vulnerable app, never a live target)
- Manipulate a message to inject markup; bypass a filter by changing the handshake; cross-site hijack to read chat history.

## Triage notes
Treat each message type as an endpoint: run the access-control matrix on them.

## Lab catalogue
3 Academy labs for this topic with levels, entry points and payload starting points: `training/academy/websockets.md`

## Automatic check (Invariant 1.1)
Finds ws:// and wss:// addresses in pages and scripts, plus common paths and socket.io. Opens the handshake with the page's own Origin (control), then with a foreign Origin while carrying the session cookie, then with the foreign Origin and no cookie. High finding only when the cookie makes the foreign-origin handshake succeed and the cookieless one is refused (cross-site WebSocket hijacking). Message-level authorization (can user A subscribe to user B's channel) is a manual test.

# Cross-site scripting: reflected, stored, DOM
Status: SEED (original notes from general technique, modelled on the public Web Security Academy topic list; not copied from it)

## Use when
User input is shown back: search, error pages, profile fields, comments, file names, rich text, markdown, emails, PDFs, admin panels, support tickets.

## Signals
- Input appears in the response or later pages; special characters are not encoded in the context where they appear.

## Verify safely (bounty-safe: smallest proof, no data dumping, no damage)
1. Send a unique marker with `<`, `>`, `"`, `'` and see which are encoded, and in which context (HTML text, attribute, JavaScript string, URL, comment).
2. Choose a context-correct payload and use a harmless proof: show a visible element or call a function that records to your own page; avoid alert in shared admin panels.
3. For stored XSS, prove with your own account and a second test account viewing it, not real users.

## Variants to try
- Contexts: tag body, attribute break-out, event handler without breaking out, `javascript:` URLs, script string break-out, template literals, JSON inside HTML, SVG.
- Filters: case variation, alternative tags and events, encoding, backticks for parentheses, strings without quotes.
- CSP bypass: allowed domains, JSONP endpoints, base tag injection, dangling markup.
- Frameworks: AngularJS expression injection, client template injection.
- Cookies are often `HttpOnly`, so show impact through actions (an authenticated request) instead.
- Blind XSS: payload that calls back from an admin view, only where the program allows.

## Lab drills (practice pattern: do these on the Academy or a local vulnerable app, never a live target)
- Reflected in HTML text; attribute; JavaScript string; stored in HTML; DOM through `document.write`, `innerHTML` and `location`; AngularJS; WAF-filtered; CSP-restricted; dangling markup; blind with callback.

## Triage notes
Severity depends on reach: self-XSS is usually out. Show the cross-account or cross-origin impact. Reflected XSS needs a working URL.

30 Academy labs for this topic with levels, entry points and payload starting points: `training/academy/cross-site-scripting.md`

# File upload, path traversal and URL-fetch SSRF
Status: SEED

Trigger: profile picture, document or import upload; "import from URL"; any parameter holding a URL or filename.

## Upload
- Allowed type check: upload a harmless `.html` or `.svg` with a marker string (not a shell). If it is stored and served from the app origin with a type that renders, that is stored XSS or content spoofing. Try double extension `a.php.jpg` and a content-type mismatch.
- Size: one slightly large file (a few MB of padding), not a flood. Accepted with no limit is a low finding.
- Filename: send `../` in the multipart filename. Look at the returned path or fetch it back. A path that reflects your traversal means arbitrary write or overwrite risk. Use a unique harmless name.
- Unsafe naming: predictable or user-controlled names allow overwrite of other users' files. Upload twice with the same name from two accounts.

## URL import (SSRF)
1. Point it at a URL you control or a unique collaborator-style host, if the program allows. A hit proves server-side fetch.
2. Internal reach, only where the program permits internal probing: loopback `http://127.0.0.1:<app port>/`, link-local metadata `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`, and the app's own internal-looking routes. Read one document to prove reach, then stop.
3. Bypass ideas when blocked: decimal or hex IP, `localhost` alias, `@` userinfo, redirects from an allowed host, DNS names resolving to private IPs. See `recon-notes/url-parser-differentials.md`.
4. Impact framing: metadata credentials, internal admin routes, reading local files through `file://` if accepted.

Control: the same request with an obviously blocked or invalid URL, showing the normal rejection.

# Card-not-present, 3-D Secure and tokenization
Status: SEED

## Use when
The target accepts cards online, issues cards, or runs a 3DS or tokenization service.

## 3-D Secure checks
- Is 3DS enforced server-side, or can the client send a "skip" or lower authentication flag? Change `eci`, `cavv`, `xid`, `3ds_status`, `authentication_status` values in the callback or the authorize request.
- Authentication result bound to the transaction? Take a valid result from one transaction and attach it to another (amount, merchant, card).
- Fallback: forcing a 3DS version downgrade or failure to a non-3DS path.
- OTP step: length, expiry, retry limit, reuse, delivery in response. See `logic/standards-and-business-rules.md`.

## Tokenization and stored cards
- Token scope: does a token from one customer or merchant work for another (BOLA)? Are tokens guessable or sequential?
- Raw PAN returned in list or detail responses; masking done in the browser only.
- CVV stored after authorization (must never be stored); CVV not required on repeat payments where it should be.
- Card enumeration: an endpoint that tells valid from invalid cards without limit (card testing). Report the missing rate limit and the oracle, using your own test numbers only.

## Issuer-side features (bank apps)
Card controls (freeze, limits, online or international use): authorization per card id, server-side enforcement, mass assignment of `limit`, `is_frozen`. PIN set and change: current PIN required, retry limit, PIN or CVV in the response. Virtual cards: see `fintech/cards-bills-merchant.md`.

## Compliance hints (for the report, not for testing shortcuts)
Storing sensitive authentication data after authorization and transmitting PAN unencrypted map to PCI DSS; cite the requirement the program or bank uses.

# ISO 8583, card switches, ATM and POS host interfaces, HSM
Status: SEED

## Use when
You are assessing a bank's card processing path: issuer host, acquirer host, switch, ATM and POS drivers, EMV, PIN handling, hardware security modules. Normally an internal or lab assessment with explicit permission. Never test a production authorization path with real cards.

## The message in one minute
A message has an MTI (0100 authorization request, 0110 response, 0200 financial request, 0210 response, 0400 and 0420 reversal and advice, 0800 network), a bitmap, and data elements: 2 PAN, 3 processing code, 4 amount, 7 transmission time, 11 STAN, 12/13 local time and date, 14 expiry, 18 merchant category, 22 entry mode, 35 track 2, 37 RRN, 38 authorization code, 39 response code, 41 terminal id, 42 merchant id, 43 name and location, 49 currency, 52 PIN block, 55 EMV data, 64 or 128 MAC.

## Tests in an authorized lab
- Message authentication: is the MAC verified on every message from every endpoint? Change amount (4) and keep the MAC; remove field 64; replay with a fresh STAN. A switch that accepts unauthenticated financial messages from any connected terminal is Critical.
- Field trust: terminal id, merchant id, acquiring institution and channel fields supplied by the peer and trusted. Can a POS driver send a terminal id belonging to a different merchant, or a processing code that is not permitted for its profile (cash advance, refund, balance enquiry)?
- Duplicate and replay handling: same STAN, RRN and date resubmitted; reversals for transactions that never existed; reversal after settlement; second reversal; advice messages that force an approval (0220 or 0420 treated as authoritative). Time window and idempotency rules.
- Response code handling: the front end or ATM driver that treats a missing or malformed field 39 as approval; timeouts that dispense cash and are never reversed. Test timeout and partial-failure paths, not only the happy path.
- Amount and currency: field 4 and 49 consistency with the terminal's currency; decimal exponent errors; amounts of zero or maximum; cashback and tip adjustments above limits.
- Offline and floor limits (POS), stand-in processing: what the switch approves when the host is down; limits in stand-in mode; whether the fallback can be triggered by the attacker.
- Entry mode and EMV: fallback to magnetic stripe, CVM downgrade, offline PIN bypass handling in the host rules (what does the issuer do with an approved fallback transaction?).
- PIN handling: PIN blocks must be encrypted under a PIN key from the terminal to the HSM; translation between zones; allowed formats (ISO format 0, 1, 3, 4). Format 0 depends on the PAN; format 1 has no PAN; unsafe translation or logging of clear PINs is Critical. Look in logs, dumps and debug traces for clear PIN blocks and track data (PCI forbids storage of track and PIN data after authorization).
- HSM and key management: separate keys per purpose (PIN, MAC, data, key encryption); no single key shared across environments (test and production); key ceremonies with split knowledge and dual control; command exposure (HSM host commands reachable from application servers beyond the necessary set; a command set that includes exporting keys in clear or translating PIN blocks between arbitrary keys is a known abuse route); use of key blocks (TR-31) versus variants; HSM management ports and default credentials on the network.
- Network: switch listeners reachable from segments that should not see them; plain TCP with no TLS on the interface; test and production switches on the same network; admin consoles of the switch exposed (see `server-side/default-credentials-and-admin-interfaces.md`).
- Logging and monitoring: card data in logs, no alert on unusual reversal ratios or terminals sending impossible processing codes.

## Standards to cite
PCI DSS (storage and transmission of card data), PCI PIN, PCI P2PE and the card scheme rules for your network. Reports to a bank carry more weight when each finding names the requirement it breaks.

## Not covered here
Physical ATM attacks (jackpotting, skimmers, black boxes) and malware on terminals need a separate physical and endpoint assessment.

# Mobile money, wallets and USSD
Status: SEED

## Use when
Wallets, mobile money (MTN MoMo, Vodafone Cash, AirtelTigo Money, M-Pesa style), USSD banking, agent cash-in and cash-out, wallet-to-bank links, airtime and data purchases.

## Wallet API tests
- BOLA on wallet id, phone number, transaction id, statement. Own wallet versus another account's.
- Amount rules: negative, zero, tiny fractions, rounding (send 0.001 many times), maximum and minimum limits, daily limits enforced server-side, fee computed on the server.
- Balance race: parallel debit, withdraw and transfer (`race`); two transfers against one balance.
- Idempotency: the same transaction reference twice must not move money twice; reference chosen by the client must be unique per account and not reusable across accounts.
- Name lookup before transfer: returns full legal name, balance or KYC data for any number (enumeration and PII exposure); rate limit on lookups.
- Reversal and failed-transaction handling: failed debit still credits the receiver; reversal request by the receiver.
- Bill and airtime purchase: price taken from the client, wrong product mapping, discount codes.
- PIN: length, retry limit and lockout, PIN in logs, PIN in the response, PIN verified on the client only, PIN reset flow (see `authn/password-reset.md`) through SIM swap assumptions.
- Linking wallet to bank or card: confirmation OTP binding to the right account and amount; linking someone else's number without their consent.

## USSD and SMS
- Session hijack assumptions: the session id or short code parameters in the aggregator callback; replaying a callback with another MSISDN (the phone number field is trusted).
- The callback endpoint from the telco aggregator should be authenticated (signature, IP allowlist); test with no auth from your own system.
- Menu injection: input that breaks menu state or reaches back-end parameters (SQL or command injection in free text fields).
- OTP and PIN delivery by SMS: content, expiry, reuse.

## Agent and merchant channels
Agent float and commission calculation, cash-in with a fake reference, merchant payment confirmation without checking the callback. Back-office roles: see `fintech/internet-banking-testing.md`.

## Proof
Two own wallets, small amounts, before and after balances, timestamps. Never move other people's money.

# Open banking, partner and B2B APIs
Status: SEED

## Use when
Bank or fintech APIs exposed to third parties: account information, payment initiation, consent screens, API gateways, partner portals, sandbox environments.

## Tests
- Consent: scope on the token versus what the endpoint returns; token for account A used on account B; consent revoked but token still works; consent screen parameters (`accounts`, `permissions`, `expiry`) tamperable after approval.
- OAuth and mTLS: redirect URI matching, state, PKCE, client authentication downgrade (client secret only where certificates are required), certificate not tied to the client id.
- Payment initiation: amount, creditor account and reference changed between initiation and authorization; payment executed without authorization; idempotency on payment id.
- Rate limits and quotas per partner key; one key reading other partners' data.
- Sandbox: real data in sandbox, sandbox credentials accepted on production, production tokens valid on sandbox.
- Gateway layers: authorization done in the gateway only, so calling the backend host or an alternate route skips it (see `authz/alternate-paths-and-derived-assets.md`); header injection into backend identity headers (`X-User-Id`, `X-Consumer-Username`) when the gateway does not strip them.
- Partner onboarding portals: self-registration that grants a production key; key rotation; keys in emails.
- Logging and audit: partner ids in logs, replayable requests.

## Evidence
Tokens and consents from your own test partner and customer; response differences with the control.

# Payment gateway and checkout testing
Status: SEED

## Use when
Checkout, card payment, hosted payment page, payment API, redirect to a gateway and back.

## Flow to map first
Cart or order created -> amount fixed where? -> redirect or iframe to the gateway -> gateway result -> callback to the server (server to server) and browser return -> order marked paid. Bugs live where the server trusts the browser leg.

## Tests (own test cards, sandbox or small real amounts only with permission)
- Amount tamper: change amount, currency or order id in the redirect parameters or the initiation request. The server must recompute from its own order.
- Currency confusion: pay 1 unit of a cheap currency for a price in an expensive one; change currency after the amount is fixed.
- Success return trust: open the "success" return URL directly, without paying, with your own order id. If the order becomes paid, that is Critical for any shop or biller.
- Signature or hash check: gateways sign requests (hash of fields with a merchant key). Change a field and keep the hash; check the server verifies on return. Look for the merchant key in client code.
- Payment status polling: can you set the status in a client parameter (`status=success`)?
- Double spending: one payment applied to two orders; one order paid twice and credited twice; use `race` for parallel return calls.
- Order id predictability and reuse: pay a small order, then replay the success token for a large order.
- Refund and cancel routes: callable by the buyer? See `payments/refunds-chargebacks-and-reversals.md`.
- Test mode leaking to production: sandbox keys or test card numbers accepted on the live site.
- Card data handling: PAN or CVV in logs, URLs, responses, local storage; card number stored by the merchant. Card-not-present details in `payments/card-not-present-and-3ds.md`.
- Third-party scripts on payment pages (skimming risk): list scripts and their hosts; a script from an uncontrolled domain on the payment page is worth reporting with its inclusion path.

## Proof
Two requests and the order state before and after, on your own account. Never use real cards you do not own.

## Patterns seen in public write-ups (own words; read from titles and short summaries only)
- Response manipulation: the browser relays the gateway's "paid" answer to the server, and the server believes the browser. Changing a failed response to a success in the proxy marks the order paid. Verify the server asks the gateway itself.
- Success-URL access: the confirmation URL returns the paid state or a download key without checking payment.
- Idempotency edge: a small change to a payment or order request with a reused idempotency key created a free order on a food-delivery platform. Replay the order request with the same key and a changed basket.
- Value mismatch: paying a small amount and receiving credit for a larger one when the credit amount comes from a client field.
- Mobile leaks: API endpoints and keys found in the Android app that unlock paid content, and exported activities exposing payment data (see `mobile/deep-links-and-webviews.md`).
- Subscription gates enforced only in the app UI: the paid set or page is retrievable by calling its API directly.

## Practice targets for banking and payments (legal, built to be attacked)
Run intentionally vulnerable bank apps such as the community "Vulnerable Bank" project locally to rehearse cards, bill payment, race and BOLA tests before touching a real system.

# Refunds, reversals and chargeback logic
Status: SEED

## Use when
Refund, cancel, void, reversal, dispute, credit note, "return" features, merchant dashboards, back-office tools.

## Tests
- Who can call refund: buyer account, merchant staff with low role, another merchant (BFLA and BOLA). Call the route with your own order and with another account's order id.
- Amount checks: refund greater than the payment; negative refund (becomes a charge, or credits the buyer); repeated partial refunds that sum above the total; refund after the order already got a full refund.
- Currency: refund in a different currency or at a different rate.
- State machine: refund of an unpaid or failed order; refund of a delivered digital good while keeping access; cancel after shipment; reversal of a transfer that was already withdrawn.
- Race: two refund requests in parallel (`race`), compare total refunded.
- Refund destination: can the refund target a different card or account than the payment? Is the destination parameter client-controlled?
- Loyalty and promo: refunds that keep coupons, points or cashback.
- Idempotency keys: same key, different amount; key reuse across accounts.

## Evidence
Order id, amounts before and after, the ledger or statement entries for both parties. State financial impact in plain numbers.

# USSD banking and USSD gateway security
Status: SEED (written from general experience with telco-integrated banking, not from a lab run)

## Use when
The bank or wallet offers a short code (`*711#`, `*170#`, `*123*4#`), a USSD menu, or an SMS-driven service. In Ghana and much of Africa this is the channel with the largest customer base and the weakest application-layer scrutiny.

## How it works (the trust chain you are testing)
Handset -> telco USSD gateway (USSD GW over SS7 or Diameter) -> an HTTP or SMPP hop to the bank's USSD application (often through an aggregator) -> core banking. The telco tells the bank's application who is calling by passing the MSISDN. The handset-to-gateway leg is not end-to-end encrypted. The application layer must therefore never treat "MSISDN says so" as authentication for money movement.

## What you can test as an application assessor (authorized, own numbers)
1. Callback authentication. The gateway calls an HTTP endpoint with fields such as `sessionId`, `msisdn` or `phoneNumber`, `serviceCode`, `text` (cumulative input joined by `*`), `networkCode`. Call it yourself with no authentication, a wrong source IP, and a different MSISDN. If the app answers and acts for an arbitrary MSISDN, anyone who can reach the endpoint can impersonate any subscriber. This is the most important USSD finding class. Prove with a read-only action on your own second number (balance enquiry), not a transfer from someone else.
2. MSISDN as the only factor. Which actions need a PIN? Balance and mini-statement without PIN leak data; transfers, airtime for others and loan requests should require a PIN every time, not only at session start. Check that the PIN is verified server-side per sensitive action and that a session flag cannot be reused by replaying the callback with the same `sessionId` and a new `text`.
3. `text` parsing. Input is a `*`-delimited path. Inject extra `*` segments to jump menu levels (skipping the PIN or confirmation step), send values out of range, negative or huge amounts, many decimals, letters in numeric fields, very long strings, `#`, and characters that reach SQL or downstream XML (see `injection/sqli-safe-verification.md`, `injection/other-injection-classes.md`). Menu state kept in the client-sent `text` instead of server state is the classic skip-step bug: send the final confirm segment directly.
4. Dial-string shortcuts. Codes like `*123*PIN*amount*recipient#` put the PIN in a string that handsets, operator logs, aggregator logs and CDRs record. If the bank supports PIN-in-string, report it as a data exposure with the recorded locations you can show.
5. Session handling. Reuse of an old `sessionId` after timeout; two concurrent sessions for one MSISDN; state left half-completed when the session times out after debit and before credit (see `fintech/core-banking-integration-and-ledger.md`). A timeout must roll back or leave an idempotent pending state.
6. Replay and idempotency. Replay a confirmed callback: does money move twice? Is there a transaction reference per request and is it unique across channels?
7. Rate and abuse. PIN guessing per MSISDN with lockout; enquiry flooding (cost to the bank per USSD session); SMS notification flooding; airtime or bill purchase loops at small amounts.
8. Notifications and receipts. SMS confirmations that include full balance or account numbers; confirmation sent to the number in the request rather than the registered number.
9. Registration and PIN reset. First-time PIN set by anyone who knows the MSISDN and an ID number (see `fintech/kyc-onboarding-and-account-opening.md`); PIN reset using the same weak data; reset notifications to the old device.
10. Aggregator hop. Credentials between aggregator and bank (basic auth, API key) in headers or config; test the bank endpoint directly, bypassing the aggregator, from outside the telco network. If it is reachable from the internet, it must authenticate the caller.

## Out of scope for application testing, but write it in the report as a risk
SIM swap, SS7 interception and USSD session hijacking at the signaling layer, malicious USSD codes (device-level). You cannot test these as an app assessor and must not try; they argue for step-up controls, SIM-swap checks and transaction limits (see `fintech/sim-swap-and-telco-dependency.md`).

## Tooling
`python3 tools/ussd_test.py --url <callback> --code '*800#' --code '*800*4001#' --own-msisdn <yours> --other-msisdn <second number you own> --confirm-own-numbers --preset africastalking` (or `hubtel`, `generic`). It walks the menu read-only, skips entries that look like money movement, and checks callback authentication, session binding, data before PIN, error leakage, throttling and (opt-in, one attempt on your own account) wrong-PIN handling. Extended dial strings such as `*800*4001#` are split into the base code and the initial text the way gateways send them.

The ITU FIGI security workstream's report on USSD and STK testing also lists device and network tests for SIM swap, SIM clone, binary over-the-air attacks (SIMjacker, CVE-2019-16256), remote USSD execution through a connected device and SS7 interception; those need lab setups and the operator's consent and are outside application testing.

## Evidence
Callback request and response with your own numbers, before and after balances, the log of menu paths, and screenshots of the SMS received.

# Banking features: cards, bills, merchant APIs, loans
Status: SEED

Trigger: virtual cards, funding, currency conversion, bill payments, merchant or checkout APIs, loans.

## Virtual cards
- BOLA: card ids are sequential. For every card route (view, freeze, limit update, fund, transactions) call it with another account's card id. Control: your own card.
- Limits: send a negative, zero, huge or non-numeric `limit`. Extra body fields on create and update-limit (`balance`, `is_frozen`, `user_id`): mass assignment.
- Funding and conversion: if the request carries a currency, rate or converted amount, change it (rate 1000 for a weak currency, fund 1 USD and receive more). The server should compute the rate.
- Predictable card numbers: create two or three of your own and look at the pattern. Plaintext number and CVV in list responses is data exposure.
- Races: fund or spend in parallel with `race` (n up to 20) and compare balances before and after.

## Bill payments
- Amount validation: negative, zero, huge, many decimals. Biller and category ids: injection probes (see `injection/sqli-safe-verification.md`) and BOLA on payment history and reference numbers. Reference numbers that are sequential allow lookup of other users' payments.
- Same payment twice with the same reference: idempotency.

## Merchant payment APIs
- Registration and login responses that return API keys or secrets. Keys in plaintext responses are exposure; test whether a key from one merchant reads another merchant's payments (BOLA).
- Raw card numbers and CVV accepted by the API, missing replay protection (send the same payment twice), verbose decline reasons, predictable authorization codes.

## Loans and approvals
Request amount bounds (negative, huge). Approval routes reachable by the requester (see `authz/bfla-admin-and-forged-claims.md`). Request, then approve from the same account.

## Always
Record balances before and after every money action, for both sides, so the finding proves the effect.

# Core banking integration, ledger and settlement logic
Status: SEED

## Use when
The app front end sits on a core banking system, a switch, a card processor or a ledger service. Flaws often appear at the join, not in either system.

## Partial failure and consistency
- Timeout after debit: does the front end retry and double-post? Does a failed credit leave the debit? Look for a reversal or reconciliation path and whether the customer can trigger it repeatedly.
- Idempotency key per transaction reference: reuse, collision across customers, client-chosen references.
- Duplicate submit: double-click, replay of the final confirm request, browser back.
- Pending states: a pending transfer that can be cancelled after the receiver already received value.

## Ledger rules
- Debits equal credits: after each test action check both sides.
- Rounding and precision: amounts with many decimals, exchange rates applied twice, rounding in the customer's favor accumulating over many small transfers (report as a business logic flaw with a small proof).
- Negative amounts and zero amounts reversing direction.
- Currency conversion: rate source, spread, the rate shown versus the rate applied, conversion between accounts of the same customer in a loop.
- Fees: waived by parameters, charged on the wrong side, rounded to zero.
- Interest, overdraft and limits: computed on the server from the ledger, not from client fields.
- Dormant or closed accounts accepting credits or debits.

## Interface layers
- Message formats (JSON, SOAP, ISO 8583 wrappers): fields the front end passes through unchanged can reach the core: processing codes, terminal ids, channel ids, reversal flags, `mti`. If the API accepts channel or terminal ids from the client, test whether a privileged channel can be selected.
- Injection into downstream queries: SQL, XPath, LDAP in names and references (see `injection/sqli-safe-verification.md`, `injection/other-injection-classes.md`).
- Error messages naming core products, hosts, stored procedures, usernames.
- Service accounts: API keys between layers exposed in config, JS or repositories.

## Reporting
Prove with a minimal sequence on test accounts and give the invariant that broke ("every debit has a credit", "a reference moves money once").

files.text:
# Fraud controls, velocity rules and monitoring review
Status: SEED

## Use when
An audit or red-team style review of whether a bank or fintech would notice and stop abuse that your technical findings enable. A finding is only as serious as the controls around it.

## Questions that change severity
1. Velocity: are there limits on number and value of transfers per hour and per day per customer, per beneficiary, per device, per IP? Are they enforced server-side with a shared counter (not per node)? Can parallel requests slip past the counter?
2. New-beneficiary controls: cooling period, lower limit for the first 24 hours, notification to the customer on a separate channel.
3. Device and session risk: new device, new geography, impossible travel, rooted or emulated device, headless client. Does the app send signals and does the server use them?
4. Step-up: which actions require a second factor, and is it bound to the action and amount (see `fintech/internet-banking-testing.md`)?
5. Reconciliation and detection: does the bank reconcile switch, core and ledger daily, and how fast does a one-sided entry get noticed? Are mismatches alerted?
6. Alerting: customer alerts for logins, transfers, limit changes, beneficiary changes, password and phone changes. Staff alerts for admin actions, bulk exports, role changes.
7. Admin and back-office: four-eyes on high-value or sensitive changes, session recording, access reviews, break-glass accounts, privileged actions logged immutably.
8. Logging quality: can you reconstruct who did what from the logs? Are logs free of secrets, signed or shipped off-host, retained long enough?
9. Incident response: is there a contact for abuse reports, a kill switch to disable a channel, a card, a wallet or a partner key within minutes?
10. Abuse of legitimate features: refunds, reversals, loan top-ups, bonus credits, agent float, bulk payments. Automation detection on these.

## How to use it in a report
For each technical finding add a short "controls that would limit this" paragraph with what you observed (present, missing, bypassable) and the residual risk. Programs and auditors both rate better-argued findings higher and fix them faster.

# Internet and mobile banking testing
Status: SEED

## Use when
Customer banking portal, mobile banking app, corporate banking, back-office admin tools. Written for authorized testing of a bank by its own security team or under a program.

## Authentication and session
- Login: username enumeration, lockout, captcha, device binding, "remember this device" token scope, password policy, reset by SMS or email, security questions.
- Step-up for risky actions: adding a beneficiary, changing limits, changing phone, large transfer. Check the step-up is enforced server-side on the API, not just in the UI, and that the OTP is bound to the action and amounts (OTP for a 10 transfer reused for a 10,000 transfer).
- Session: fixation, concurrent sessions, timeout, token after logout, token in URL, cookies flags, back button after logout showing data.
- Transaction signing: what exactly is signed? If the signed data is not the final beneficiary and amount, the signature does not protect the transaction.

## Transfers and payments
- Own accounts, same-bank, inter-bank, international: amount, currency and fee computed on the server; beneficiary name and account tampered after validation (check the final request, not the form).
- Account number as an id: BOLA on source account (debit another account), on statements, on standing orders, on cheque books, on card lists.
- Limits: daily and per-transaction limits applied per user, not per session; change the limit with a parameter; parallel requests to exceed.
- Beneficiaries: add without approval, add through a CSRF-able request, edit a beneficiary after approval, beneficiary limits.
- Scheduled and recurring payments: edit another user's schedule; run in the past; amounts changed after approval (maker-checker bypass).
- Maker-checker in corporate banking: the same user acting as both roles, approval of own request, approval by tampering `approver_id`, role field accepted from the client.

## Statements, documents, notifications
- Statement and receipt downloads by predictable id or file name; PDF generation SSRF; CSV export formula injection (see `web/csv-and-formula-injection.md`).
- Notification settings: change the contact phone or email without step-up; SMS content leaking balances.

## Back office and admin
Admin portals on the same host or a sibling host; default credentials; role checks on every function; export of all customers; impersonation features; audit log editing; direct object access to customer KYC documents.

## Integration points
Core banking and switch interfaces behind the API (ISO 8583 style messages, SOAP, MQ): injection of fields passed through, error messages with core system names, timeouts that leave a debit without a credit (partial failure handling). See `fintech/core-banking-integration-and-ledger.md`.

## Reporting
Use plain financial impact: who could move how much, with which preconditions. Redact account numbers. Use only your own test customers and approved test accounts.

files.text:
# KYC, onboarding and account opening
Status: SEED

## Use when
Self-service account opening, identity verification, document upload, liveness checks, limits by KYC tier.

## Tests
- Tier enforcement: limits and features of a higher KYC tier reachable with a lower tier (change `kyc_level`, `tier`, `verified` in requests; call higher-tier endpoints directly).
- Verification state set by the client: `is_verified`, `status=approved` accepted in onboarding calls (mass assignment).
- Document handling: the uploaded ID image reachable by predictable URL without authorization (BOLA on files); EXIF and metadata; stored in a public bucket (see `cloud/storage-buckets-and-object-stores.md`); file upload flaws (see `server-side/file-upload.md`).
- Identity lookup abuse: national ID, phone or BVN-style lookups that return full personal data for any number; rate limits on lookups.
- Duplicate and synthetic identities: same ID with different phone, same phone across accounts, one document for many accounts.
- Liveness and selfie checks: result computed on the client and trusted; reuse of an old successful session id; endpoint that accepts any image after a successful challenge id.
- Phone and email verification: see `logic/verification-flaws.md`.
- Sanctions and PEP checks skipped through alternate onboarding channels (agent, USSD, corporate flow).
- Referral and sign-up bonuses: self-referral, bulk account creation, bonus before KYC.

## Data protection
Personal data sent to third-party scripts, stored unencrypted, kept after rejection, shown in full in lists and logs. Mention the data protection law that applies (Ghana Data Protection Act, 2012 for Omni BSIC) when rating privacy findings.

files.text:
# SIM swap, number recycling and telco dependency
Status: SEED

## Use when
The bank trusts a phone number for authentication, OTP delivery, mobile money, USSD or notifications. Very common in West African banking.

## Why it matters
Whoever controls the number controls the OTP, the USSD session and password resets. SIM swap fraud, number recycling (a deactivated number reissued to a stranger) and insider swaps are the dominant real-world account takeover route for mobile-money-linked accounts.

## What the application owner should have, and what to test for
- SIM-swap signal: the bank queries the telco (or an aggregator service) for a recent swap or device change before high-risk actions, or imposes a cooling period after the number changes. Test: does the app behave any differently for a number that was changed 5 minutes ago? You can only examine the app's side: documented controls, config flags, responses that mention swap checks.
- Phone number change flow (see `authn/account-takeover-chains.md`): needs strong step-up that does not depend on the old phone alone (ID document, branch, in-app biometric on a bound device), and notifies old contacts.
- Recycled numbers: a customer who closed a number but kept the account; the new owner of the number requests a reset. Is there a re-verification cadence?
- OTP binding: OTP valid for one action, one amount and one beneficiary; OTP content shows the amount and recipient so the user can spot manipulation; short expiry; no reuse across channels.
- Trusted device: binding to the device is a compensating control. Check whether the app can register a new device with only an SMS OTP (then SIM swap defeats it).
- Limits and cooling: new device or new beneficiary limits (for example a daily cap for 24 hours), velocity rules, delayed first large transfer.
- Alerts: push or email alert for changes to phone, device, limits and beneficiaries, sent to a channel that a SIM swap does not control.

## Report
Frame as risk and control gaps, not as an exploit. State what a fraudster who has the victim's number can do end to end, listing the app's steps, and which compensating control stops each step.

# OS command injection
Status: SEED (original notes from general technique, modelled on the public Web Security Academy topic list; not copied from it)

## Use when
A value is passed to a system utility: ping or DNS tools, image or PDF converters, file names, git or archive features, stock or report generators, anything that shells out.

## Signals
- Error output looks like shell text (`sh: 1:`, `command not found`), a filename or host is echoed in an error.
- Response time depends on the input in odd ways.

## Verify safely (bounty-safe: smallest proof, no data dumping, no damage)
1. Inject a harmless separator test: `;`, `&&`, `|`, newline, backticks, `$()`, and check for a behaviour difference.
2. Prove with a delay (`sleep 5` or `ping -c 5 127.0.0.1`) against a zero-delay control, three runs.
3. Or prove with `id` or `whoami` output if the response shows it. Stop there.

## Variants to try
- Blind: time delay, redirect output to a web-readable file only where allowed, DNS callback to your own host.
- Separators differ by platform (Windows uses `&`, `|`, `||`).
- Space filtering: `${IFS}`, tabs, brace expansion. Quote and keyword filters: split strings, wildcards.
- Argument injection when the command is fixed but arguments are controlled (leading dash options).

## Lab drills (practice pattern: do these on the Academy or a local vulnerable app, never a live target)
- Simple output-visible injection.
- Blind with time delay.
- Blind with output redirection.
- Blind with out-of-band callback and data in the lookup name.

## Triage notes
Critical when proven. Show only the harmless command output or the delay. Never read secrets, never keep a shell.

# NoSQL injection (operators and syntax)
Status: SEED (original notes from general technique, modelled on the public Web Security Academy topic list; not copied from it)

## Use when
JSON bodies or query strings that look like Mongo-style filters: login, search, `{"user":...}`, parameters like `filter[name]=`.

## Signals
- Request fields accepted as objects; error text mentions Mongo, BSON, `$where`, or a JavaScript error.
- Quote or `\` changes the response in a string field.

## Verify safely (bounty-safe: smallest proof, no data dumping, no damage)
1. Syntax check: a single quote, then a balanced payload; compare to control.
2. Operator check: replace a string value with an object such as `{"$ne": null}` in JSON, or `field[$ne]=x` in a query string; see if the check passes without the real value.
3. Prove with a login for your own test account whose password you pretend not to know, or a search that returns your own object only.

## Variants to try
- Boolean conditions through JavaScript in `$where` (always-true and always-false pair).
- `$regex` to confirm a field value character by character (practice only).
- Extract a field name length, then characters, only for your own account.
- Operator injection in nested objects and arrays; content type switch from form to JSON to reach operators.
- Time delay with a busy loop in `$where` where blind.

## Lab drills (practice pattern: do these on the Academy or a local vulnerable app, never a live target)
- Detect syntax injection in a category filter and show hidden items.
- Bypass authentication with an operator.
- Extract a field from your own user with a boolean script.
- Discover a hidden field name through operator errors.
- Extract data with `$regex`.

## Triage notes
Impact is auth bypass or cross-account read. State the operator used and the control request. Do not brute force other users' fields.

files.text:
# Other injection classes: LDAP, XPath, expression language, template, header, log
Status: SEED

## Use when
Search or login forms backed by directories (LDAP, Active Directory), XML data stores, Java apps (Spring, JSF) with expression language, report builders, mail templates, any place user text is evaluated by a back-end interpreter.

## LDAP injection
Probes in login or search fields: `*`, `)(`, `*)(uid=*`, `admin)(&)`. A login that succeeds with `*` as a password, or a search that returns all entries, proves it. Check error messages naming the directory.

## XPath injection
Probes: `'`, `' or '1'='1`, `' or ''='`. Login and lookup against XML stores. Error messages naming XPath functions confirm.

## Expression language and template evaluation
- Java EL, SpEL, OGNL, MVEL: `${7*7}`, `#{7*7}`, `%{7*7}`; look for `49` in responses. Spring: errors showing `SpelEvaluationException`.
- Server-side templates: see `advanced/ssti.md`. Client templates (AngularJS) in older apps: `{{7*7}}`.
- Prove with arithmetic only; do not run commands.

## Header, log and format injection
- CRLF: `web/crlf-and-header-injection.md`.
- Log forging: newline plus fake log lines in a field that is logged (affects audit trails and SIEM parsing).
- Format strings in languages that use them with user input (`%s%s%s`, `{0}`), JSON and XML injection into downstream requests (a name that closes a JSON string and adds a field: `","role":"admin`).
- SSI and server-side includes: `<!--#exec cmd=...-->` in file uploads and fields on legacy servers; prove with an `echo` of a date directive (`<!--#echo var="DATE_LOCAL"-->`).
- NoSQL, SQL and command injection have their own notes in this folder.

## Report
The input, the observable evaluation (arithmetic result, directory entry count, injected field), and the data or function reachable.

files.text:
# SQL injection: detection, union, blind, out-of-band
Status: SEED (original notes from general technique, modelled on the public Web Security Academy topic list; not copied from it)

## Use when
A value reaches a database: login, ids, sort or filter fields, search, headers (User-Agent, Referer), cookies (tracking ids), JSON fields, GraphQL arguments.

## Signals
- A single quote or a backslash changes the response or gives a database error; two quotes put back to normal.
- `1 AND 1=1` and `1 AND 1=2` give different pages; `1+1` or `2-1` behaves like `2`.
- Response time moves with a conditional delay.

## Verify safely (bounty-safe: smallest proof, no data dumping, no damage)
1. Send the quote and the doubled quote, note status, length and body difference against a control.
2. Boolean pair (true and false conditions) must differ in a repeatable way, three times.
3. For proof of read access, extract one harmless value (database version or current user), not user tables.
4. Time-based: use a short delay (3 to 5 s) and a control with zero delay; repeat to rule out network noise.

## Variants to try
- Number of columns: `ORDER BY n` until error, or `UNION SELECT NULL,...`; find a text column; read version with the dialect function.
- Dialects: version functions and comment styles differ (`--`, `#`, `/**/`); string concatenation differs (`||`, `+`, `CONCAT`).
- Blind: boolean with substring or length tests; time with a conditional sleep; errors with a failing cast that leaks the value.
- Out of band: DNS or HTTP callback through a database function, only to a collaborator host you control and only if the program allows it.
- Second order: payload stored in one request and used in another (profile name used in a report query).
- Filter bypass: case, comments inside keywords, URL or double encoding, JSON unicode escapes, XML entity encoding of the payload.
- Different contexts: inside quotes, numeric, ORDER BY (no quotes), INSERT or UPDATE values, LIKE patterns.

## Lab drills (practice pattern: do these on the Academy or a local vulnerable app, never a live target)
- Retrieve hidden rows by breaking a WHERE condition.
- Log in as a known user by commenting out the password check.
- UNION: find column count, then a string column, then read one value.
- Blind boolean: confirm a single known value character by character (practice only).
- Conditional error and time-delay variants.
- Out-of-band interaction using a callback host.
- Filter bypass with XML encoding.

## Triage notes
Report the injectable parameter, the boolean or error difference, and the version string. Do not enumerate customer tables. Many programs pay only for proven read or auth bypass; a bare error with no differential is often informative at best.

# SQL injection: safe verification
Status: SEED

Trigger: any parameter that looks like it reaches a query: login fields, ids in path, search, filters, category ids, sort, GraphQL arguments, headers.

Prove, do not extract.
1. Error differential: send a single quote `'` then two `''` in the parameter. A 500 or database error on one and clean on two is a strong signal. Detailed errors that name the database engine are also an information disclosure finding.
2. Boolean differential: `x' AND '1'='1` vs `x' AND '1'='2` (or numeric `1 AND 1=1` vs `1 AND 1=2`). Different bodies or lengths with the same status = injectable. Keep the pair as proof and control.
3. Auth bypass in login: the classic `' OR '1'='1' --` as username with any password. One request. Control: the same body without the injection fails. Success returns an identity you do not own: stop there, do not enumerate users.
4. Time based only if 1 and 2 give nothing, one request with a short delay (2 to 3 seconds), compared with a control.
5. Never dump tables, never read other users' rows beyond one record shown by the bypass itself, never use stacked queries that write or drop. State this in the report.

Where to look in banking and shop apps: login, biller or category lookups by id, transaction search, merchant or card lookups, GraphQL resolver arguments, order and invoice filters.

# Backend-as-a-service and CMS exposure (Directus, Strapi, Hasura and similar)
Status: DISTILLED

## Use when
A host answers like a headless CMS or a managed backend: `/server/info`, `/items/`, `/files`, `/admin`, `/api/` with collection names, GraphQL with generated types, PocketBase `/api/collections`, Firebase `*.firebaseio.com/.json`, CouchDB `/_all_dbs`, Elasticsearch `/_cat/indices`.

## What the autopilot does (read-only)
Directus: `/server/info`, `/files?limit=1`, `/users?limit=1`, `/collections`. Strapi, PocketBase, Hasura, CouchDB, Elasticsearch, Parse and Firebase RTDB have one or two read-only probes each. A finding needs a real response with data shaped like the product, not just a 200.

## Manual follow-up (with permission, test accounts only)
1. For each readable collection, ask for one record only (`limit=1`) and describe the fields, never export the table.
2. Check the same collection with no token, a low-privilege token and another tenant's token. A public role that can read is a configuration problem; a low role that reads other users' rows is broken access control.
3. Check write: only against your own test record, with an update that you revert. Do not create or delete on shared data.
4. File libraries: list metadata first. Download only your own test file to prove access.

## Severity
Unauthenticated read of personal data or database exports is usually High (a program may call it Critical when it is bulk personal data of many people). Unauthenticated write, credentials that lead to admin, or code execution is Critical. See `rules/severity-calibration.md`.

## Report
Show the unauthenticated request and response (redacted), the number of records reachable if the API tells you (do not enumerate), the fix (turn off public read, scope the role, rotate leaked credentials).

files.trigger: Any host, content discovery, hidden parameters, fuzzing method
files.text:
# Content discovery, parameter discovery and fuzzing
Status: DISTILLED

Trigger: any host. Run it after the sweep, before deep testing, and again after you learn the stack.

## What the autopilot does
1. Calibrates first: requests four paths that cannot exist and records status, size, word count and redirect shape. A hit must differ from that, so single-page apps that answer 200 for everything do not flood the result.
2. Walks a wordlist (built-in 436 words, or a SecLists file downloaded under Account and security, chosen with the `fuzz_wordlist` option). Requests are light: not stored unless they hit. Each hit is promoted with one normal request so it has evidence and passes the leak and exposure scanners.
3. Tries backup variants (`.bak`, `.old`, `~`) of discovered files.
4. Hidden parameters: sends 40 candidate names at once with a marker value and bisects when the response changes, so a list of 300 names costs a few dozen requests. Reflection of the marker is flagged as an injection lead.
5. Stays inside scope, the request budget and the per-host delay. Lower the delay only on systems you own.

## Reading results
- 200 with unique content: look at it. 401 or 403: the path exists, so try other methods, a trailing slash, case changes, and header tricks (`X-Original-URL`, `X-Forwarded-For`) only if the program allows it.
- 500: the path exists and breaks on empty input, which is often a lead for parameters.
- Same size as the catch-all: ignore.

## Manual fuzzing tips
- Tune the wordlist to the stack: api-endpoints for APIs, raft files for directories, burp-parameter-names for parameters.
- Fuzz one thing at a time: path segment, extension, parameter name, parameter value, header, method.
- Filter by size and word count, not only status. Re-check hits with a normal browser request before reporting.
- Never fuzz login, reset or payment endpoints with real accounts; use your own test accounts and the rate-limit rules of the program.
